Learning latent user/item factors (SVD-style, ALS) to fill the sparse matrix — the classic recsys workhorse.
🎥 Watch: Search 'matrix factorization recommender systems'.
💻 Code: Implement matrix factorization with gradient descent on a ratings dataset.

units.title: Content-based & hybrid
units.text:
Using item features (and embeddings) for cold-start, and hybrid systems that blend CF + content.
🎥 Watch: Search 'content based vs collaborative filtering hybrid'.
💻 Code: Add a content-based model and blend it with your CF into a hybrid recommender.

units.title: Implicit feedback & ranking
units.text:
Clicks/views (implicit) vs ratings, ranking losses (BPR), and the top-N recommendation framing.
🎥 Watch: Search 'implicit feedback recommender BPR'.
💻 Code: Train an implicit-feedback ranker and generate top-N recommendations.

units.title: Recommender evaluation
units.text:
Offline metrics (precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MAP), the offline/online gap, and coverage/diversity.
🎥 Watch: Search 'recommender system evaluation metrics'.
💻 Code: Evaluate your recommenders with precision@k + NDCG and compare them fairly.

units.title: End-to-end recommender system
units.text: [Block A] Pick a real interactions dataset (MovieLens etc.) and build CF + matrix-factorization baselines. [Block B] Add content features for cold-start and a hybrid ranker for implicit feedback. [Block C] Evaluate with ranking metrics and serve top-N via a small API — a portfolio recsys project.
units.demo: Production recommender system (collaborative + matrix factorization + hybrid), served via API.

units.title: Systems that personalize
units.text: Collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, content/hybrid, implicit ranking and evaluation are the recommender toolkit. Re-read your offline-vs-online caveat.
units.mastery: How does matrix factorization fill a sparse ratings matrix, and why can offline metrics mislead you about a live recommender?

units.title: Containers & Docker for ML — a just-in-time primer
units.text:
Just enough containers to productionize ML now: images, layers, Dockerfiles, volumes, and reproducible environments — a bridge to the deep Containers/Kubernetes track later. (Full ML system design is its own week soon.)
🎥 Watch: Docker in 100 Seconds; Docker for Data Science/ML tutorials.
💻 Code: Containerize a training + inference script with a slim multi-stage Dockerfile; build, run, and push the image to a registry.

units.title: Experiment tracking (MLflow, W&B)
units.text:
Tracking params/metrics/artifacts for reproducibility and comparison instead of losing results in notebooks.
🎥 Watch: MLflow quickstart; Weights & Biases tutorials.
💻 Code: Instrument a training script with MLflow (params, metrics, model) and compare runs in the UI.

units.title: Model registry & versioning
units.text:
Registering models with stages (staging/production), versioning, and promoting the right model to serving.
🎥 Watch: MLflow Model Registry docs.
💻 Code: Register your model, version it, and promote a version to 'production' via the registry.

units.title: Reproducible ML pipelines
units.text:
Turning notebooks into reproducible pipelines (scripts, configs, seeds, environments) so results are rebuildable.
🎥 Watch: Made With ML — reproducibility; search 'reproducible ML pipeline'.
💻 Code: Refactor a notebook into a config-driven, seeded training pipeline that runs end to end.

units.title: Data & model versioning (DVC)
units.text:
Versioning datasets and models alongside code with DVC, so an experiment is fully reconstructable.
🎥 Watch: DVC docs/tutorial.
💻 Code: Version a dataset + model with DVC and reproduce a past experiment from a git+dvc checkout.

units.title: MLflow-tracked training pipeline
units.text: [Block A] Build a reproducible, config-driven training pipeline (data -> features -> train -> evaluate). [Block B] Instrument it with MLflow (params/metrics/artifacts) + DVC data versioning, and register the best model. [Block C] Document how to reproduce any run from git + dvc — a portfolio MLOps foundation piece.

units.title: From notebook to system
units.text: System design, experiment tracking, registry/versioning, reproducibility and DVC turn ad-hoc modeling into engineering. Reproduce an old run to prove it works.
units.mastery: What makes an ML experiment reproducible, and what does a model registry give you that a folder of pickles doesn't?

units.title: Serving (FastAPI, BentoML)
units.text:
Wrapping a model in an API, request/response schemas, and packaging with BentoML for standardized serving.
🎥 Watch: Search 'FastAPI ML model serving'; the BentoML docs.
💻 Code: Serve your model behind a FastAPI endpoint with a typed request/response and validation.

units.title: Batch vs online inference
units.text:
Precomputed batch predictions vs low-latency online inference, and the latency/cost/freshness tradeoffs.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen — batch vs online; search 'batch vs online inference'.
💻 Code: Implement both a batch scoring job and an online endpoint for the same model; compare latency.

units.title: Monitoring: drift & performance
units.text:
Data drift, concept drift, and monitoring live performance/latency — models decay silently without it.
🎥 Watch: Search 'ML model monitoring data drift'; the Evidently AI docs.
💻 Code: Add drift detection (e.g. Evidently) + latency/throughput metrics to your service.

units.title: Shadow & A/B deployment
units.text:
Rolling out models safely: shadow (mirror traffic), canary, and A/B testing model versions in production.
🎥 Watch: Search 'shadow deployment canary ML'.
💻 Code: Add a shadow-mode path that scores with a new model without affecting responses; log the comparison.

units.title: CI/CD for ML
units.text:
Automated testing, model-validation gates, and deployment pipelines (CML/GitHub Actions) for models.
🎥 Watch: Search 'CI/CD for machine learning'; Made With ML — CI/CD.
💻 Code: Wire a CI pipeline that tests, validates the model against a threshold, and deploys on pass.

units.title: Deploy a model as an API with monitoring
units.text: [Block A] Serve your model via FastAPI/BentoML with schemas, containerized. [Block B] Add monitoring: drift detection, latency/throughput metrics and alerting, plus a shadow-mode path. [Block C] Wire CI/CD with a model-validation gate and deploy — a flagship MLOps portfolio project.
units.demo: ML model served as an API with drift monitoring and CI/CD.

units.title: Keeping models alive
units.text: Serving, batch vs online, monitoring, safe rollout and CI/CD are what keep a model useful after launch. Re-check that your drift monitor fires.
units.mastery: How would you detect that a live model has silently degraded, and what's your safe path to ship a replacement?

units.title: Designing ML systems (a framework)
units.text:
Framing an ML problem: objective, constraints, data, baseline, metrics, and the design-doc discipline.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen — Designing ML Systems; search 'ML system design interview'.
💻 Code: Write a full ML design doc for a realistic problem (fraud/recsys/churn).

units.title: Scaling training: distributed & data-parallel
units.text:
Data vs model parallelism, and scaling training across GPUs/nodes when data or models don't fit.
🎥 Watch: Search 'distributed training data parallel explained'.
💻 Code: Run a data-parallel training job (PyTorch DDP or Spark ML) and measure the scaling.

units.title: Feature/label pipelines at scale
units.text:
Building training data at scale, point-in-time correctness, and label generation / weak supervision.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen — training data; search 'weak supervision Snorkel'.
💻 Code: Build a point-in-time-correct training set from event logs (no future leakage).

units.title: Cost & latency tradeoffs
units.text:
Model size vs accuracy vs latency vs cost, caching predictions, and choosing the cheapest thing that works.
🎥 Watch: Search 'ML inference cost optimization'.
💻 Code: Profile inference cost/latency and cut it (quantization/caching/simpler model) within an accuracy budget.

units.title: Case studies: fraud, recsys
units.text:
Reading real ML system designs (feature pipelines, serving, feedback loops) to build pattern intuition.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Uber Michelangelo' and 'Netflix recommendations system design'.
💻 Code: Reverse-engineer a public ML system design into a diagram + tradeoff notes.

units.title: ML system-design doc + a prototype
units.text: [Block A] Choose a realistic problem and write a full system-design doc (objective, data, features, model, serving, monitoring, tradeoffs). [Block B] Prototype the core: a training pipeline + a served model + basic monitoring. [Block C] Present it as a design doc + working prototype — exactly the artifact senior ML interviews want.

units.title: Thinking at system scale
units.text: Problem framing, distributed training, scaled data pipelines, cost/latency and case studies build ML system-design judgment. Re-read your design doc critically.
units.mastery: Walk an interviewer through your ML system design: objective, data, baseline, serving, monitoring, and the top three tradeoffs.

units.title: Problem framing & data
units.text:
Pick a real, meaningful ML problem; define the objective and metric and assemble/clean the data.
🎥 Watch: Revisit Chip Huyen's framing + your EDA notes.
💻 Code: Write the capstone problem statement and success metric, and load/clean the data.

units.title: Feature & label pipelines
units.text:
Build leak-free feature and label pipelines with point-in-time correctness.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your feature-engineering + feature-store work.
💻 Code: Build the feature/label pipeline with tests and no future leakage.

units.title: Modeling & evaluation
units.text:
Baseline -> improved model with honest cross-validation, the right metric, and error analysis.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your evaluation toolkit.
💻 Code: Train baseline + improved models, evaluate rigorously, and do error analysis.

units.title: Serving
units.text:
Serve the model as an API with schemas, containerized, ready for monitoring.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your serving + MLOps work.
💻 Code: Serve the model (FastAPI/BentoML), containerized, with a typed API.

units.title: Monitoring & writeup
units.text:
Add drift/performance monitoring and write the portfolio narrative + model card.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your monitoring + interpretability work.
💻 Code: Add monitoring, write the README/model card, and record a demo.

units.title: ML-product capstone — build & ship
units.text: [Block A] Assemble the full ML product: data -> features -> model -> API, reproducible and tracked (MLflow/DVC). [Block B] Add monitoring (drift, performance), interpretability (SHAP) and CI/CD. [Block C] Ship it: repo, model card, demo — your flagship Data Science / ML portfolio project.
units.demo: End-to-end ML product: data → features → model → served API with monitoring.

units.title: Phase 2 review
units.text: You've gone from math to a shipped, monitored ML product. Step back: which parts felt weakest, and how will the AI phase build on this foundation?
units.mastery: Give the 3-minute tour of your ML product: the problem, the data/features, why this model, and how you'd know if it broke in production. Spaced recall (no notes): explain three Data-Engineering ideas you'd started to forget — an LSM-tree, a Kafka consumer group, and a star schema.

units.title: MLPs & universal approximation
units.text:
You built and trained neural nets in the CV track; here the foundations get rigorous and general. Universal approximation: why an MLP with one hidden layer can represent any continuous function — and what that promise does NOT give you (it says nothing about learnability or generalization). Width vs depth as competing ways to add capacity.
🎥 Watch: 3Blue1Brown — Neural Networks ch.1; Michael Nielsen — 'A visual proof that neural nets can compute any function'.
💻 Code: Empirically test universal approximation: fit a wiggly 1D function with MLPs of increasing width and depth, and chart where each helps.

units.title: Autograd engines, deeply
units.text:
You've called .backward(); now build the thing behind it. Reverse-mode autodiff is a graph algorithm: record ops, topologically sort, and chain local gradients backward. Building a real micrograd once means no framework's autograd is ever magic again.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'The spelled-out intro to neural networks' (building micrograd); 3Blue1Brown — backpropagation calculus.
💻 Code: Build a tiny autograd engine (values, ops, topological backward) and train an MLP on tabular data; verify its gradients numerically against finite differences.

units.title: Activations & initialization
units.text:
ReLU/GELU/sigmoid/tanh and why they matter (vanishing gradients); why init (Xavier/He) makes training even possible.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — makemore (activations, init, batchnorm); search 'weight initialization deep learning'.
💻 Code: Compare training with different activations + inits and watch gradients vanish or explode.

units.title: Loss functions & optimizers (Adam)
units.text:
Cross-entropy vs MSE, and the optimizers (SGD, momentum, RMSProp, Adam) that shape convergence.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Adam optimizer explained'; Karpathy — makemore.
💻 Code: Train the same net with SGD vs Adam and compare convergence.

units.title: Regularization: dropout & batchnorm
units.text:
Dropout, batch/layer norm, weight decay and early stopping — the tricks that make deep nets generalize and train stably.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — makemore (batchnorm); search 'dropout batchnorm explained'.
💻 Code: Add dropout + batchnorm to your net and measure the effect on overfitting.

units.title: Neural net from scratch (NumPy) then PyTorch
units.text: [Block A] Build a full MLP from scratch in NumPy on a tabular dataset: forward, backprop, an optimizer, a training loop — kept off images so it complements (not repeats) your CV CNN. [Block B] Reimplement it in PyTorch and match the results; note exactly what the framework automates (autograd, optimizers) versus your hand-rolled version. [Block C] Write up 'what a neural net really computes' with your from-scratch code — it proves deep understanding.

units.title: What a network really computes
units.text: Neurons/MLPs, backprop, activations/init, losses/optimizers and regularization are the machinery of every deep model. Re-run your micrograd and watch the gradients flow.
units.mastery: Explain backprop as reverse-mode autodiff, and why initialization and normalization matter for training.

units.title: Data-parallel training (DDP)
units.text:
You gained single-GPU PyTorch fluency in the CV track; now scale it out. Data-parallel replicates the model across GPUs, splits the batch, and all-reduces gradients so every replica stays in sync. DDP (not the old DataParallel) is the standard, and knowing when data-parallel is enough saves a lot of complexity.
🎥 Watch: PyTorch — 'DistributedDataParallel' tutorial; 'Distributed training explained'.
💻 Code: Convert a training script to DDP and run it multi-process on a single GPU to prove the mechanics; verify results match the single-process run.

units.title: Sharding: FSDP & ZeRO
units.text:
When the model itself won't fit, shard it: ZeRO/FSDP split parameters, gradients and optimizer states across devices. The memory math — weights + grads + Adam states (the 4x surprise) + activations — tells you exactly what to shard and why a 7B model laughs at a 4 GB card.
🎥 Watch: 'ZeRO / FSDP explained'; PyTorch — 'FSDP tutorial'.
💻 Code: Write the memory formula for weights+grads+Adam states of a given model; wrap a model in FSDP and observe the per-device memory drop.

units.title: Large-batch training & LR scaling
units.text:
Bigger batches change optimization: the linear LR-scaling rule, warmup to avoid early divergence, and gradient accumulation as a poor-man's big batch. Schedules (cosine, one-cycle) squeeze out the last accuracy.
🎥 Watch: 'Large-batch training explained'; 'LR warmup + cosine schedule'.
💻 Code: Sweep batch size with matched LR scaling and chart convergence; reproduce the linear-scaling rule and find where it breaks.

units.title: Profiling & debugging at scale
units.text:
Speed is a bottleneck hunt: compute vs memory vs data-loading vs communication. The PyTorch profiler finds the real culprit; Karpathy's recipe finds the training bug (loss won't drop, NaNs, silent throughput loss).
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'A Recipe for Training Neural Networks'; 'PyTorch profiler' walkthrough.
💻 Code: Profile a training run, identify the bottleneck, and cut step time; then break a run (bad LR, no shuffle) and diagnose each issue from the curves.

units.title: Reproducibility & experiment tracking
units.text:
Research-grade rigor: seeds, deterministic ops, config management, and tracking runs (MLflow/W&B) so results are comparable and reproducible. Untracked experiments are unpublishable and unshippable.
🎥 Watch: 'Reproducible deep learning'; 'W&B / MLflow for experiments'.
💻 Code: Add seeding + a config system + experiment tracking to your trainer; log three runs and compare them side by side.

units.title: Scale & optimize a training run
units.text: [Block A] Make a real training script distributed-ready with DDP, proving correctness by matching single-process results; add FSDP-style memory savings where the model benefits. [Block B] Optimize: profile to find the bottleneck, then apply large-batch + LR scaling + mixed precision and cut wall-clock per step — measure every change. [Block C] Report: a scaling + optimization writeup (throughput, memory, convergence) backed by experiment tracking — research rigor on a recruiter-friendly systems topic.
units.demo: Distributed, profiled, optimized training run with a scaling report (DDP + FSDP + mixed precision).

units.title: Training that scales
units.text: Data-parallel, sharding, large-batch optimization, profiling and reproducibility turn a single-GPU trainer into a scalable one. Re-profile and confirm the win is real, not luck.
units.mastery: Where does the VRAM go when you train, what exactly do FSDP/ZeRO shard, and what's your first move when throughput is low or the loss won't drop?

units.title: Graphs as data
units.text:
So much real data is graphs: molecules, social networks, knowledge graphs, code, transactions. Nodes, edges, node/edge features and adjacency define the structure; tasks come in three flavours — node-level, edge/link-level, and graph-level. Flattening a graph to a table throws away the relationships that carry the signal.
🎥 Watch: Petar Velickovic — 'Intro to Graph Neural Networks'; DeepFindr — 'GNN' series (intro).
💻 Code: Represent a small graph (adjacency + node features) in PyTorch Geometric and networkx; compute degree/centrality stats and frame one node-, link- and graph-level task.

units.title: Message passing & GCN
units.text:
The core GNN idea: each node aggregates messages from its neighbours and updates its embedding — repeated, information flows across the graph. The GCN layer is the canonical instance; stacking too many layers causes over-smoothing (every node looks the same).
🎥 Watch: 'Graph Convolutional Networks explained'; DeepFindr — 'Message passing'.
💻 Code: Implement one message-passing layer from scratch, then train a GCN in PyG for node classification on Cora; show accuracy collapse as you stack too many layers.

units.title: GraphSAGE & GAT (attention on graphs)
units.text:
Scaling and expressiveness: GraphSAGE samples a fixed set of neighbours so training scales to huge graphs; GAT puts attention over neighbours (the attention you built for ViT, now on graph edges). Different aggregators, different inductive biases.
🎥 Watch: 'GraphSAGE explained'; 'Graph Attention Networks (GAT)'.
💻 Code: Train GAT on a citation graph and compare against GCN; inspect which neighbours a node attends to.

units.title: Graph-level tasks & pooling
units.text:
For graph classification (e.g. predicting a molecule's property) you pool node embeddings into one graph embedding via a readout (mean/max/attention pooling). This is how GNNs power drug discovery and materials screening.
🎥 Watch: 'Graph pooling explained'; a molecular-property-prediction GNN walkthrough.
💻 Code: Do graph classification on a small molecular dataset (a TUDataset) with global pooling; compare readout functions.

units.title: Where GNNs matter & geometric DL
units.text:
Use-cases: recommenders, fraud rings, knowledge-graph reasoning (ties straight to your RAG/GraphRAG work), molecules. Geometric deep learning is the unifying lens — CNNs, transformers and GNNs are all networks that respect a symmetry of the data (grid, sequence, graph).
🎥 Watch: Michael Bronstein — 'Geometric Deep Learning' overview talk.
💻 Code: Build a link-prediction model on a knowledge graph (predict missing edges) — a direct echo of grounding an LLM with structured knowledge.

units.title: Graph ML on a real network
units.text: [Block A] Pick a real graph — citation, molecular, or a knowledge graph from your RAG work — and frame a node-, link-, or graph-level task with a clean PyG data pipeline. [Block B] Train and compare GCN vs GraphSAGE vs GAT with a leakage-free split (edges must not straddle train/test), and evaluate with the right metric for the task. [Block C] Ship: a repo + writeup on exactly when graph structure beats treating the data as flat tabular — a distinctive, research-flavoured portfolio piece.

units.title: Learning on graphs
units.text: Message passing, GCN/SAGE/GAT, graph-level pooling and the geometric-DL lens add a whole data modality most engineers skip. Re-run your model and check for edge leakage in the split.
units.mastery: Explain message passing in one paragraph, why stacking many GNN layers causes over-smoothing, and when graph structure beats a flat tabular model.

units.title: Pixels, channels & image formation
units.text:
An image is a grid of pixels: one number (grayscale) or three (RGB) in [0,255] at 8-bit depth. Resolution, channel count and bit depth define the tensor you'll feed a model. A quick tour of image formation — light -> lens -> sensor -> array — grounds why exposure, noise and colour even exist, and why a 'clean scan' is a modelling assumption, not a given.
🎥 Watch: First Principles of Computer Vision (Shree Nayar) — 'Image Formation'; Computerphile — 'How Digital Images Work'.
💻 Code: Load a photo; print shape, dtype, min/max; display the R/G/B channels separately; build grayscale by hand as a weighted channel sum and diff it against cv2.cvtColor.

units.title: Arrays & tensors — the HWC vs CHW trap
units.text:
The #1 shape bug in real repos: OpenCV/NumPy hand you HxWxC, PyTorch wants CxHxW. Cropping, indexing and slicing are just array ops; strides and views explain why some ops copy and some alias. Batching stacks images into NCHW — the shape every training loop speaks.
🎥 Watch: Aladdin Persson — 'PyTorch tensor basics'; skim the NumPy array-basics and PyTorch tensor docs.
💻 Code: Convert an image HWC<->CHW with permute/transpose; crop by slicing; stack 4 images into an NCHW batch; deliberately break a shape and read the traceback to fix it.

units.title: Colour spaces & the OpenCV BGR betrayal
units.text:
RGB vs BGR (why OpenCV betrays you), HSV (colour separated from brightness) and grayscale. Colour space is a modelling choice: HSV beats RGB for 'find the red object under changing light' because hue is stable when illumination isn't.
🎥 Watch: Sentdex — 'OpenCV colour spaces'; First Principles of CV (Nayar) — 'Colour'.
💻 Code: Read with OpenCV, fix BGR->RGB before showing in matplotlib; threshold an object in HSV; round-trip RGB->grayscale->RGB and measure what's irreversibly lost.

units.title: Normalization, resizing & interpolation
units.text:
Every repo divides by 255 and subtracts ImageNet mean/std — nets train best on zero-centred, unit-scale inputs. Resizing needs interpolation (nearest/bilinear/bicubic), each with tradeoffs; aspect-ratio squash and missing anti-aliasing are silent accuracy killers.
🎥 Watch: PyTorch — 'torchvision.transforms' walkthrough; an 'image interpolation explained' primer.
💻 Code: Write normalize(img, mean, std) and its exact inverse; resize one image with three interpolation methods and compare; reproduce torchvision Normalize+Resize and diff against it.

units.title: Reading, writing & torch Datasets
units.text:
PIL vs OpenCV vs torchvision.io — who returns what, EXIF-orientation gotchas, lossy vs lossless formats. A torch Dataset/DataLoader turns a folder of images into batched, augmented tensors — the on-ramp to every training loop in this track.
🎥 Watch: PyTorch — 'Datasets & DataLoaders' tutorial; a 'PIL vs OpenCV' overview.
💻 Code: Write a Dataset that reads an image folder, applies transforms, returns (tensor,label); wrap it in a DataLoader; visualize one augmented batch with make_grid.

units.title: Image I/O & preprocessing toolkit
units.text: [Block A] Core: a library that loads any common format to a normalized CxHxW tensor — colour-space aware (auto BGR->RGB), with configurable resize/interpolation, ImageNet normalization and its inverse for visualization. [Block B] Augmentation & batching: a torch Dataset/DataLoader over an image folder with a composable transform pipeline (flip, crop, colour-jitter) and a make_grid preview utility. [Block C] Ship: a typed API, a pytest suite (round-trip normalize/denormalize, shape invariants) and a README with before/after visuals — the first repo in your cv track.

units.title: Images are just tensors
units.text: Pixels -> channels -> tensors, HWC vs CHW, colour spaces and normalization are the substrate everything else stands on. Re-open your toolkit and fix one rough edge with fresh eyes.
units.mastery: Cold: why does img.shape differ between OpenCV and PyTorch, what exactly does /255 then minus ImageNet mean/std accomplish, and where does the BGR trap bite?

units.title: Convolution by hand
units.text:
Convolution is plain arithmetic before it's a neural layer: a kernel slides over the image, multiply-and-sum, with padding and stride deciding output size. Doing it by hand on a 5x5 patch demystifies every conv layer you'll meet later — a CNN just learns these kernels.
🎥 Watch: 3Blue1Brown — 'But what is a convolution?'; First Principles of CV (Nayar) — 'Linear Image Filters'.
💻 Code: Implement 2D convolution from scratch in NumPy (padding + stride); apply hand-made blur and sharpen kernels; verify against scipy/cv2.filter2D.

units.title: Filtering & denoising
units.text:
Smoothing (box, Gaussian, median) trades detail for noise reduction; median crushes salt-and-pepper where Gaussian smears it. Separable kernels and why a Gaussian is cheap. This is the pre-processing that decides whether downstream edges and thresholds behave.
🎥 Watch: Computerphile — 'Gaussian blur'; First Principles of CV (Nayar) — 'Image Smoothing'.
💻 Code: Add Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise to an image; denoise each with Gaussian vs median; measure which wins for which noise and explain why.

units.title: Edges: Sobel & Canny
units.text:
Edges are large intensity gradients. Sobel estimates the gradient; Canny adds non-max suppression + hysteresis to yield clean thin edges. Edges are the backbone of contour finding, document boundaries and classical feature detectors.
🎥 Watch: Computerphile — 'Canny Edge Detector' and 'Sobel Operator'; First Principles of CV (Nayar) — 'Edge Detection'.
💻 Code: Compute Sobel gradients (magnitude + direction) from your convolution; run Canny and sweep its two thresholds; overlay detected edges on the original.

units.title: Thresholding & morphology
units.text:
Binarization is the OCR-preprocessing backbone: global vs Otsu (auto) vs adaptive (for shadows/uneven light). Morphology — erode, dilate, open, close — cleans the binary mask (removes specks, closes gaps) before contours.
🎥 Watch: First Principles of CV (Nayar) — 'Binary Images'; Murtaza's Workshop — 'Thresholding & morphology in OpenCV'.
💻 Code: Binarize a shadowed document scan three ways (global/Otsu/adaptive) and justify the winner; clean it with open/close; show each step.

units.title: Contours, components & perspective warp
units.text:
Contours and connected components turn a binary mask into objects you can measure and count. A perspective transform (homography) deskews a photographed page into a flat scan — Sessions 3-4's pre-processing plus this is a full classical document pipeline.
🎥 Watch: Murtaza's Workshop — 'Document Scanner OpenCV'; First Principles of CV (Nayar) — 'Boundary Detection'.
💻 Code: Find the page contour in a phone photo, order its 4 corners, and warp to a top-down deskewed view; count connected components on a binarized page.

units.title: Document scanner (photo -> clean page)
units.text: [Block A] Pipeline: phone photo of a document -> grayscale -> denoise -> edge/contour detect -> find the page quadrilateral -> perspective-warp to a flat, deskewed page. [Block B] Binarize: adaptive/Otsu thresholding + morphology to produce a crisp, OCR-ready black-on-white page, robust to shadow and uneven lighting. [Block C] Ship: a CLI (input image -> output clean PNG/PDF), a few hard test images (shadow, skew, low contrast), and a README showing each stage — the classical backbone your document-AI week will build on.
units.demo: Classical document scanner: phone photo -> deskewed, binarized, OCR-ready page, built from convolution up.

units.title: Classical CV still runs production
units.text: Convolution-by-hand, filtering, edges, thresholding, morphology and homography are exactly what sits in front of real OCR pipelines. Re-run your scanner on a fresh hard photo and tune one weak stage.
units.mastery: Given a noisy, shadowed, skewed scan, name and order the full preprocessing chain and justify each choice — and say which stage a CNN could replace and which it can't.

units.title: Neurons, layers & activations
units.text:
A neuron is a weighted sum plus a non-linearity; stacking them makes an MLP. Activations (ReLU and friends) are what let a network model non-linear functions — without them, deep is just one big linear map. This is the vision-flavoured intro your later AI track assumes.
🎥 Watch: 3Blue1Brown — 'But what is a neural network?'; Andrej Karpathy — 'Neural Networks: Zero to Hero' (ep. 1, micrograd).
💻 Code: Build a 2-layer MLP in NumPy for a toy 2D classification set; implement forward pass and ReLU; plot the decision boundary.

units.title: Backpropagation from scratch
units.text:
Backprop is the chain rule applied over a computation graph: local gradients multiplied backward. Building a tiny autograd once (a la micrograd) means PyTorch's .backward() is never magic again.
🎥 Watch: 3Blue1Brown — 'Backpropagation, intuitively' and 'Backpropagation calculus'; Karpathy — 'micrograd' walkthrough.
💻 Code: Extend yesterday's MLP with manual backprop (compute each gradient) and train it with plain gradient descent; verify gradients numerically.

units.title: Why fully-connected fails on images
units.text:
A dense layer on a 224x224x3 image is a parameter explosion and throws away spatial structure. Convolution shares weights across space and exploits locality — the same learned kernel detects an edge anywhere. This is why CNNs, not MLPs, own pixels.
🎥 Watch: 3Blue1Brown — 'But what is a convolution?' (revisit through the learned-kernel lens); StatQuest — 'Convolutional Neural Networks clearly explained'.
💻 Code: Compute and compare the parameter count of a dense vs a conv layer on 224x224x3; implement a conv layer's forward pass and confirm weight sharing.

units.title: Pooling, stride & receptive fields
units.text:
Pooling and stride shrink spatial size and grow the receptive field so deep layers 'see' more of the image. Feature hierarchies emerge: edges -> textures -> parts -> objects. Knowing receptive-field growth explains why depth matters and where detail is lost.
🎥 Watch: Stanford CS231n — 'CNN architectures' lecture (pooling/receptive fields section); DeepLizard — 'Max pooling explained'.
💻 Code: Sketch (and compute) the receptive field growing across 4 conv/pool layers; add pooling to your conv and visualize feature maps at each stage.

units.title: CNN architectures & training a CNN
units.text:
From LeNet -> AlexNet -> VGG: deeper, smaller kernels, more channels. BatchNorm stabilizes training; the standard block is conv-BN-ReLU-pool. Now assemble a real CNN and train it end-to-end with a proper loss and optimizer.
🎥 Watch: Stanford CS231n — 'CNN architectures'; Aladdin Persson — 'CNN in PyTorch'.
💻 Code: Build a small VGG-style CNN in PyTorch and train it on CIFAR-10 with the full loop by hand (Dataset, DataLoader, forward, cross-entropy, backward, step); batch 64 fits in 4 GB.

units.title: CNN on CIFAR-10, from the training loop up
units.text: [Block A] From scratch: a small CNN (conv-BN-ReLU-pool blocks) with the entire training loop written by hand — no Lightning, no shortcuts — reaching a respectable CIFAR-10 accuracy. [Block B] Diagnose: track train/val loss curves, add augmentation and one regularizer (dropout or weight decay), and show the over/underfitting story with plots. [Block C] Ship: a clean repo (model, train, eval), a confusion matrix, and a short note tracing a single batch's shapes through every layer.

units.title: What a network really computes
units.text: Neurons, backprop, convolution-as-learned-kernels, receptive fields and a real training loop — the foundation the whole track (and your later AI track) stands on. Re-open your CIFAR CNN and narrate one batch end to end.
units.mastery: Trace one batch through your CNN on paper — shapes at every layer — and explain why a conv layer beats a dense layer on images in both parameters and inductive bias.

units.title: Tensors & autograd, deeply
units.text:
PyTorch tensors carry a device and a grad graph; autograd records ops and replays them backward. requires_grad, .backward(), and .detach()/no_grad() are the levers. Understanding the graph is how you debug 'why is my gradient None / exploding'.
🎥 Watch: PyTorch — '60-Minute Blitz' (autograd section); Aladdin Persson — 'PyTorch autograd'.
💻 Code: Recreate your CV3 backprop result using autograd and confirm the gradients match your manual ones; break the graph with .detach() and watch grads vanish.

units.title: nn.Module anatomy
units.text:
nn.Module is the unit of composition: __init__ registers layers, forward() defines the computation, parameters() and buffers (like BatchNorm stats) are tracked automatically. This is the object every repo you'll ever read is built from.
🎥 Watch: Aladdin Persson — 'PyTorch nn.Module'; Daniel Bourke — 'PyTorch for Deep Learning' (Module sections).
💻 Code: Rewrite your CIFAR CNN as clean nn.Modules (a reusable ConvBlock); print named_parameters and named_buffers and explain the difference.

units.title: Dataset, DataLoader & transforms at scale
units.text:
Real training feeds data efficiently: map-style vs iterable Datasets, num_workers, pin_memory, and transform pipelines that augment on the fly. Bottlenecks here (not the GPU) are why many training runs crawl.
🎥 Watch: PyTorch — 'Datasets & DataLoaders'; 'torchvision transforms v2' overview.
💻 Code: Build a Dataset+DataLoader for a custom folder with train/val transforms; benchmark num_workers settings; profile whether you're GPU- or data-bound.

units.title: Device, checkpoints, train/eval
units.text:
The mechanics that separate a script from a repo: .to(device), saving/loading state_dict (not the whole model), and toggling model.train()/eval() so dropout and BatchNorm behave. Forgetting eval() is a classic silent-bug.
🎥 Watch: PyTorch — 'Saving & loading models'; Aladdin Persson — 'Save/load checkpoints'.
💻 Code: Add checkpoint save/resume (model+optimizer+epoch) to your trainer; prove eval() vs train() changes BatchNorm/dropout outputs on the same input.

units.title: Mixed precision & gradient accumulation
units.text:
The 4 GB survival kit: autocast + GradScaler halve memory and speed things up; gradient accumulation simulates a big batch on a small card. Knowing where the VRAM goes (weights, grads, activations) is how you fit models that 'shouldn't fit'.
🎥 Watch: PyTorch — 'Automatic Mixed Precision' tutorial; 'Gradient accumulation explained'.
💻 Code: Add AMP + gradient accumulation to your trainer; measure the memory and speed delta; find the largest effective batch your 1650 can reach.

units.title: A reusable PyTorch training repo
units.text: [Block A] Refactor CV3 into the standard layout — model.py, dataset.py, train.py, config.yaml — with a clean CLI and logging, so any future model drops in. [Block B] 4 GB kit: mixed precision, gradient accumulation, checkpoint/resume, and a metrics logger (loss/acc curves) — everything you need to train real models on a small GPU. [Block C] Ship: run it end-to-end on a fresh dataset to prove reuse; README documents the config and the memory tricks. This repo trains every model in the rest of the track.

units.title: Fluent in the language every repo speaks
units.text: nn.Module, Dataset/DataLoader, checkpoints, train/eval and AMP are the PyTorch fluency that makes unfamiliar repos readable. Open a train.py you've never seen and narrate it.
units.mastery: Where does the VRAM go when you train, and exactly which two changes let a model that OOMs at batch 64 fit on a 4 GB card — and what do they cost you?

units.title: ImageNet, pretraining & backbones
units.text:
'Backbone' means a network pretrained on ImageNet whose features transfer. Pretraining gives you edge/texture/part detectors for free; you rarely train vision from scratch. Knowing the backbone zoo (ResNet, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt) is repo literacy.
🎥 Watch: Yannic Kilcher — 'ImageNet / transfer learning intuition'; Stanford CS231n — 'Transfer learning'.
💻 Code: Load a pretrained ResNet from torchvision; inspect its layers; run inference on your own images and read the top-5 ImageNet predictions.

units.title: ResNet in depth — residual connections
units.text:
Residual connections (x + F(x)) let gradients flow through very deep nets and turn 'learn the mapping' into 'learn the residual'. This one idea unlocked 100+ layer networks and shows up everywhere (including transformers).
🎥 Watch: Yannic Kilcher — 'Deep Residual Learning (ResNet paper)'; Aladdin Persson — 'ResNet from scratch'.
💻 Code: Implement a residual block and a small ResNet in PyTorch; ablate the skip connection (remove it) and show training degrade.

units.title: Fine-tuning vs feature extraction
units.text:
Two transfer strategies: freeze the backbone and train only a new head (feature extraction, fast, few data) vs unfreeze and fine-tune with a small learning rate (more data, higher ceiling). Discriminative learning rates and freeze-then-unfreeze schedules matter.
🎥 Watch: Aladdin Persson — 'Transfer learning in PyTorch'; fast.ai — 'Fine-tuning' lesson notes.
💻 Code: On a small custom dataset: (a) feature-extract, (b) full fine-tune, (c) freeze-then-unfreeze; compare accuracy and training time.

units.title: Augmentation & class imbalance
units.text:
Augmentation (flips, crops, colour-jitter, mixup/cutmix) is free regularization; the right set depends on the domain (don't flip digits). Imbalance distorts learning — weighted losses, resampling and the right metric fix what accuracy hides.
🎥 Watch: 'Data augmentation for images' overview; 'Handling class imbalance' (Krish Naik / StatQuest).
💻 Code: Train with vs without augmentation and plot the gap; induce class imbalance and fix it with a weighted loss; measure per-class recall.

units.title: Metrics that don't lie
units.text:
Accuracy lies on imbalanced data. Precision/recall/F1, the confusion matrix, and ROC/AUC tell the real story; the threshold is a business choice. This is how you explain 'why 95% accuracy made the client furious'.
🎥 Watch: StatQuest — 'Confusion matrix', 'ROC and AUC'; 'Precision, recall, F1 explained'.
💻 Code: Log precision/recall/F1 + a confusion matrix for your fine-tuned model; move the decision threshold and watch precision/recall trade; write the one-paragraph diagnosis.

units.title: Fine-tuned image classifier with honest metrics
units.text: [Block A] Fine-tune a ResNet (18/34) on a real custom dataset using your CV4 trainer; try feature-extraction vs full fine-tune and pick the winner on validation. [Block B] Rigor: augmentation pipeline, class-imbalance handling, and a full evaluation — confusion matrix, per-class precision/recall/F1, ROC where it applies. [Block C] Ship: a demo (upload an image -> prediction + confidence), and a README that reads the confusion matrix like a diagnosis, not a scoreboard.
units.demo: Fine-tuned image classifier with honest metrics (confusion matrix, per-class precision/recall/F1) and a live demo.

units.title: Transfer learning is the default
units.text: Backbones, residuals, fine-tune-vs-extract, augmentation, imbalance and honest metrics are 90% of applied vision. Re-read your confusion matrix and name the single change that would most help the worst class.
units.mastery: Your model hits 95% accuracy but the client is furious — walk the confusion matrix to the real failure, and say which of fine-tuning, augmentation, rebalancing or threshold-moving you'd reach for first and why.

units.title: Semantic vs instance vs panoptic
units.text:
Segmentation is per-pixel labelling. Semantic labels every pixel by class; instance separates individual objects; panoptic unifies both. Choosing the right one is a problem-framing decision that drives the whole architecture and label format.
🎥 Watch: 'Image segmentation types explained'; Meta AI — 'Segment Anything (SAM)' overview.
💻 Code: Take one labelled image and produce/visualize a semantic mask, an instance mask, and (conceptually) a panoptic one; write down which a document-understanding pipeline actually needs.

units.title: Masks, per-pixel loss & class balance
units.text:
A mask is a label image; segmentation is classification at every pixel, trained with per-pixel cross-entropy (often plus Dice loss). Background dominates, so class weighting and Dice matter even more than in classification.
🎥 Watch: DigitalSreeni — 'Loss functions for segmentation'; 'Dice loss vs cross-entropy'.
💻 Code: Implement pixel-wise cross-entropy and Dice loss; train a trivial segmenter on shapes and show why pixel-accuracy looks great while the object is missed.

units.title: U-Net in depth
units.text:
U-Net is an encoder-decoder with skip connections: the encoder captures context, the decoder recovers resolution, and skips restore fine detail lost to pooling. It's the workhorse of medical/document segmentation and returns later as the diffusion denoiser.
🎥 Watch: DigitalSreeni — 'U-Net semantic segmentation' series; Aladdin Persson — 'U-Net from scratch in PyTorch'.
💻 Code: Implement U-Net from scratch (encoder, bottleneck, decoder, skip concatenations); confirm shapes line up at every skip.

units.title: IoU, Dice & evaluating masks
units.text:
IoU (intersection over union) and Dice are the honest segmentation metrics; pixel accuracy is a liar when classes are imbalanced. Boundary quality and small-object recall are where models quietly fail.
🎥 Watch: 'IoU and Dice coefficient explained'; DigitalSreeni — 'Segmentation metrics'.
💻 Code: Compute IoU and Dice by hand for a 4x4 toy mask pair, then implement them; evaluate your U-Net and visualize best/worst predictions.

units.title: Modern segmentation: DeepLab, Mask R-CNN, SAM
units.text:
Names you'll meet in repos: DeepLab (atrous convolutions, semantic), Mask R-CNN (detection + instance masks), and SAM (promptable, zero-shot 'segment anything'). Knowing when to train a U-Net vs prompt SAM is a real 2026 decision.
🎥 Watch: Meta AI — 'Segment Anything'; 'DeepLab explained'; 'Mask R-CNN explained'.
💻 Code: Run SAM (or MobileSAM for 4 GB) on your own images with point/box prompts; compare its masks to your trained U-Net on the same objects.

units.title: Train a U-Net + benchmark against SAM
units.text: [Block A] Train a U-Net from scratch on a small segmentation set (Carvana or Oxford-Pets subset, sized for 4 GB) using your CV4 trainer; report IoU and Dice. [Block B] Compare: run SAM/MobileSAM zero-shot on the same images and put your trained model head-to-head — where does each win? [Block C] Ship: a visual gallery (input / ground-truth / U-Net / SAM), the metrics table, and a README on when you'd train vs prompt.

units.title: Seeing at the pixel level
units.text: Semantic/instance/panoptic, U-Net, IoU/Dice and the SAM era cover applied segmentation end to end. Re-open your worst predictions and hypothesize the fix (loss, augmentation, resolution).
units.mastery: Compute IoU by hand for a toy mask pair, explain why pixel accuracy lied, and say when you'd reach for a trained U-Net over prompting SAM.

units.title: Boxes, anchors & IoU
units.text:
Detection = localize + classify. Boxes are (x,y,w,h); anchors are prior boxes the model refines; IoU-for-boxes measures overlap and defines a 'correct' detection. These primitives underlie every detector, one- or two-stage.
🎥 Watch: Aladdin Persson — 'Intersection over Union' and 'Anchor boxes'; 'Object detection basics'.
💻 Code: Implement box IoU; match a set of predicted boxes to ground truth by IoU; visualize anchors of different scales/aspect ratios over an image.

units.title: NMS & mAP
units.text:
Non-max suppression removes duplicate boxes for the same object; without it you drown in overlapping detections. mAP (mean average precision) is the standard metric — precision/recall over IoU thresholds. Understanding mAP is reading-detector-papers literacy.
🎥 Watch: Aladdin Persson — 'Non-Max Suppression' and 'mean Average Precision (mAP)'.
💻 Code: Implement NMS from scratch; run it on raw model outputs and show duplicates collapse; compute AP for one class over a couple of IoU thresholds.

units.title: Two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN)
units.text:
Two-stage: a region proposal network suggests candidate boxes, then a head classifies and refines them. Accurate, heavier. The RoI-pooling idea and the proposal->refine split are the conceptual anchor for the whole family.
🎥 Watch: Yannic Kilcher / 'Faster R-CNN explained'; 'RPN and RoI pooling'.
💻 Code: Run a pretrained Faster R-CNN from torchvision on your images; inspect proposals vs final boxes; read out scores and labels.

units.title: One-stage & set prediction (YOLO, DETR)
units.text:
One-stage (YOLO/SSD) predict boxes directly on a grid — fast, real-time. DETR reframes detection as set prediction with a transformer and bipartite matching — no anchors, no NMS. The speed/accuracy/simplicity triangle.
🎥 Watch: Aladdin Persson — 'YOLO from scratch' (concepts); Yannic Kilcher — 'DETR'.
💻 Code: Run pretrained YOLOv8 inference on your images; parse the output tensor (boxes/scores/classes) yourself and draw the boxes; time it vs Faster R-CNN.

units.title: Text detection & the document bridge
units.text:
Text detection IS object detection — EAST/DBNet find text regions before recognition. This is the bridge from natural-image CV to document AI: detect regions -> recognize -> lay out, which document-AI pipelines are built on.
🎥 Watch: 'EAST / DBNet text detection explained'; a 'scene text detection' overview.
💻 Code: Run a text detector on document/scene images; visualize the detected text boxes; feed one crop into an OCR recognizer and read the text out.

units.title: Detection pipeline on your own images
units.text: [Block A] Inference pipeline: run YOLOv8 on a folder of your images, parse outputs, and render annotated results with class + confidence. [Block B] Fine-tune: train the detector on a small custom set (or a document/text-region set), and evaluate with mAP + your own NMS. [Block C] Ship: an annotated gallery, a mAP table, and a README explaining anchors, NMS and why removing NMS floods you with duplicates.

units.title: Localize, then classify
units.text: Boxes, anchors, NMS, mAP and the two-stage/one-stage/set-prediction families cover applied detection. Text-detection is the on-ramp to documents. Re-run your pipeline and eyeball the false positives.
units.mastery: Explain NMS and why removing it floods you with duplicates, and contrast how Faster R-CNN, YOLO and DETR each decide 'which boxes'.

units.title: Attention from scratch
units.text:
Attention lets every element look at every other and pull in what's relevant: queries, keys, values, a softmax over QK^T, a weighted sum of V. A tiny worked numeric example makes it concrete before any framework. This is the engine behind ViT and every LLM you'll use later.
🎥 Watch: 3Blue1Brown — 'Attention in transformers'; Umar Jamil — 'Attention explained (coded)'.
💻 Code: Work a 2-token self-attention by hand given small Q/K/V matrices; then implement scaled dot-product attention in PyTorch and reproduce your hand result.

units.title: Multi-head attention & positional encoding
units.text:
Multiple heads attend to different relationships in parallel; positional encodings inject order that attention alone lacks (images have no inherent sequence, so patches get positions). Together they make a transformer permutation-aware.
🎥 Watch: Umar Jamil — 'Multi-head attention coded'; 'Positional encoding explained'.
💻 Code: Extend your attention to multi-head; add learned positional embeddings; visualize a head's attention map over tokens.

units.title: The transformer block
units.text:
A transformer block = attention + MLP with residual connections and LayerNorm around each. That's it, repeated. Recognizing this pattern makes ViT, BERT and GPT the same shape with different inputs and heads.
🎥 Watch: Umar Jamil — 'Transformer block coded'; Peter Bloem — 'Transformers from scratch'.
💻 Code: Implement a full transformer encoder block (attn -> add&norm -> MLP -> add&norm); stack a few and confirm shapes are preserved.

units.title: Vision Transformers (ViT)
units.text:
ViT cuts an image into patches, linearly embeds them as tokens, prepends a CLS token, adds positions, and runs a transformer — classification reads the CLS token. It shows convolution's inductive bias isn't required if you have enough data.
🎥 Watch: AI Coffee Break — 'Vision Transformer (ViT)'; Yannic Kilcher — 'An Image is Worth 16x16 Words'.
💻 Code: Build a tiny ViT forward pass by hand (patch-embed -> +positional -> +CLS -> transformer blocks -> CLS head) and print shapes at each stage.

units.title: CNN vs ViT & hybrid backbones
units.text:
CNNs bring locality and data efficiency; ViTs bring global context and scale better with data/compute. 2026 reality: hybrids (ConvNeXt, Swin) and 'it depends on data size'. Knowing the tradeoff picks the right backbone for a job.
🎥 Watch: 'ConvNeXt / Swin Transformer explained'; 'CNN vs ViT' comparison talk.
💻 Code: Fine-tune a pretrained ViT (timm) on your CV5 dataset and compare accuracy, data-efficiency and speed against your ResNet.

units.title: ViT: build it, then fine-tune it
units.text: [Block A] From scratch: a working (tiny) ViT — patch embedding, positional + CLS tokens, transformer blocks, classification head — trained on a small dataset to prove it learns. [Block B] Fine-tune a pretrained ViT on your CV5 dataset with your CV4 trainer; head-to-head vs ResNet on accuracy, data-efficiency and latency. [Block C] Ship: attention-map visualizations, the comparison table, and a README on when you'd pick CNN vs ViT vs hybrid.
units.demo: Vision Transformer built from scratch and fine-tuned, benchmarked head-to-head against a ResNet.

units.title: Attention is the engine
units.text: Attention, multi-head, positional encoding, the transformer block and ViT are shared across all of modern AI — you'll meet them again in the LLM track. Re-derive attention from Q/K/V without notes.
units.mastery: Explain how a 224x224 image becomes a sequence of tokens, work a 2-token attention by hand, and say when a ViT beats a CNN and why.

units.title: Why self-supervision
units.text:
Labels are expensive; the internet is huge and unlabelled. Self-supervised learning invents a task from the data itself (predict a missing patch, match augmented views) to learn representations that transfer with little labelled data. This is how modern vision scales.
🎥 Watch: Yannic Kilcher — 'Self-supervised learning overview'; 'SSL in computer vision' primer.
💻 Code: Set up a linear-probe evaluation harness: freeze a pretrained encoder, train only a linear head, and measure how good its features are on your dataset.

units.title: Contrastive learning & InfoNCE
units.text:
Contrastive learning pulls positive pairs together and pushes negatives apart in embedding space; the InfoNCE loss formalizes it. Temperature and negatives matter. This objective underlies SimCLR and CLIP.
🎥 Watch: Yannic Kilcher — 'SimCLR'; 'Contrastive learning / InfoNCE explained'.
💻 Code: Implement the InfoNCE loss; on a small set, build positive pairs by augmentation and train a tiny encoder; watch same-image views cluster.

units.title: SimCLR, augmentation & collapse
units.text:
SimCLR shows augmentation choice IS the algorithm — strong, well-chosen augmentations make or break the learned features. Representation collapse (everything maps to one point) is the failure mode; understanding how methods avoid it is the point.
🎥 Watch: 'SimCLR explained'; 'Understanding representation collapse'.
💻 Code: Ablate SimCLR augmentations (remove colour-jitter / crop) and measure linear-probe accuracy drop; demonstrate a collapse case.

units.title: Masked autoencoders (MAE)
units.text:
MAE masks most of the image and trains a ViT to reconstruct the missing patches — a generative self-supervised task that scales beautifully with transformers. It's BERT for pixels, and a strong pretraining recipe.
🎥 Watch: 'Masked Autoencoders (MAE) explained'; Yannic Kilcher — 'MAE'.
💻 Code: Load a pretrained MAE encoder; visualize reconstructions at high mask ratios; linear-probe its features against SimCLR's on your data.

units.title: CLIP & zero-shot
units.text:
CLIP trains image and text encoders into one shared space with a contrastive loss over image-caption pairs. Result: zero-shot classification via text prompts, and the 'eyes' that get bolted onto LLMs (your VLM week). Prompt wording matters.
🎥 Watch: Umar Jamil — 'CLIP explained and coded'; Yannic Kilcher — 'CLIP'.
💻 Code: Zero-shot classify your own images with open_clip using text prompts; compare against your CV5 fine-tuned model on the same classes; probe how prompt phrasing moves accuracy.

units.title: Zero-shot CLIP vs your fine-tuned model
units.text: [Block A] Zero-shot: classify your CV5 dataset with open_clip and a set of engineered text prompts — no training — and report accuracy. [Block B] Head-to-head: compare zero-shot CLIP against your fine-tuned ResNet/ViT; find where zero-shot wins (rare/new classes) and where fine-tuning wins. [Block C] Ship: a small contrastive-training demo (your InfoNCE encoder), the comparison writeup, and a README on when to reach for zero-shot vs fine-tune vs SSL-pretrain.

units.title: Learning without labels
units.text: Self-supervision, contrastive/InfoNCE, SimCLR, MAE and CLIP are how modern vision gets its representations — and CLIP is the bridge to multimodal AI. Re-run your zero-shot harness and tune the prompts.
units.mastery: State the InfoNCE idea in words, and decide for three scenarios (new class weekly / 200 labelled images / millions unlabelled) whether you'd use zero-shot CLIP, fine-tuning, or SSL pretraining.

units.title: Autoencoders & VAEs
units.text:
An autoencoder compresses to a latent and reconstructs; a VAE makes that latent a distribution you can sample, giving a smooth generative space. The reparameterization trick and the KL term are the core ideas — and VAEs live on inside latent diffusion.
🎥 Watch: Aladdin Persson — 'Variational Autoencoder from scratch'; 'VAE explained'.
💻 Code: Train a small VAE on MNIST; sample new digits from the latent; interpolate between two digits and watch the latent space morph.

units.title: GANs & mode collapse
units.text:
A GAN pits a generator against a discriminator in a minimax game; at equilibrium the generator makes realistic samples. Training is unstable and mode collapse (generator makes one thing) is the classic failure. In 2026 GANs survive in niches; diffusion won images.
🎥 Watch: Aladdin Persson — 'GAN from scratch'; Computerphile — 'Generative Adversarial Networks'.
💻 Code: Train a small DCGAN on a simple set; deliberately trigger and then mitigate mode collapse; compare sample diversity.

units.title: Diffusion: forward & reverse
units.text:
Diffusion adds noise step by step (forward) then learns to denoise step by step (reverse). The network predicts the noise; sampling starts from pure noise and denoises to an image. This is the DDPM core that powers Stable Diffusion.
🎥 Watch: Outlier — 'Diffusion models explained'; Umar Jamil — 'DDPM from scratch'.
💻 Code: Implement the forward noising schedule; visualize an image degrading to noise; train a tiny denoiser on MNIST and sample from noise.

units.title: The U-Net denoiser & latent diffusion
units.text:
The denoiser is a U-Net (CV6 returns) conditioned on the timestep. Latent diffusion runs the whole process in a VAE's compressed latent space instead of pixels — the trick that made Stable Diffusion runnable on consumer GPUs.
🎥 Watch: Umar Jamil — 'Stable Diffusion from scratch'; 'Latent diffusion explained'.
💻 Code: Trace the shapes through a latent-diffusion pipeline (VAE encode -> denoise in latent -> VAE decode); identify where each component from earlier weeks reappears.

units.title: Stable Diffusion & text conditioning
units.text:
Text conditioning uses a CLIP text encoder (CV9) to steer denoising via cross-attention; classifier-free guidance controls how strongly. Prompting, seeds, and step count are the levers. On 4 GB: fp16 + attention slicing / --medvram.
🎥 Watch: Computerphile — 'Stable Diffusion'; 'Classifier-free guidance explained'.
💻 Code: Run quantized Stable Diffusion 1.5 locally (fp16 + attention slicing to fit 4 GB); sweep guidance scale and steps; document what each knob does.

units.title: VAE from scratch + local Stable Diffusion
units.text: [Block A] Train a VAE on MNIST end to end (your CV4 trainer): reconstructions, samples, and a latent-space interpolation gif. [Block B] Run Stable Diffusion 1.5 locally under 4 GB (fp16 + attention slicing); build a small prompt/guidance/steps study showing how each affects output. [Block C] Ship: a gallery of generations, the latent-interpolation demo, and a README explaining forward/reverse diffusion and exactly what the U-Net predicts.
units.demo: VAE from scratch + Stable Diffusion 1.5 running locally on a 4 GB GPU, with a prompt/guidance study.

units.title: Making images, not just reading them
units.text: Autoencoders, VAEs, GANs and diffusion (incl. latent diffusion + text conditioning) complete the generative side of vision — and the U-Net and CLIP you already built power it. Re-run SD locally and explain each knob to a rubber duck.
units.mastery: Explain forward vs reverse diffusion, state exactly what the U-Net predicts, and say why latent diffusion — not pixel diffusion — is what fits your 4 GB card.

units.title: OCR anatomy end to end
units.text:
OCR is a pipeline, not a model: text detection -> recognition -> layout analysis -> reading order -> table structure. Each stage is a CV problem you've already met. Knowing the stages is how you debug a bad extraction to the right component — the core of real document-AI work.
🎥 Watch: 'How OCR works' overview; 'Document layout analysis explained'.
💻 Code: Run an OCR engine (Tesseract or PaddleOCR) on a real document; dump the per-stage intermediates (boxes, text, layout) and inspect where errors originate.

units.title: Where classical CV plugs in
units.text:
Your CV2 preprocessing (deskew, binarize), CV6 segmentation (layout/table regions) and CV7 detection (text regions) are exactly the front of an OCR system. Mapping them makes the whole document stack legible instead of magic.
🎥 Watch: 'Table detection & structure recognition'; revisit Murtaza — 'Document scanner' with fresh eyes.
💻 Code: Chain your CV2 scanner -> a text detector -> a recognizer on a hard document; measure how much your preprocessing improves the final text.

units.title: Docling internals
units.text:
Docling converts PDFs/images to structured content by orchestrating several models (layout, table, OCR). Understanding which models it runs — and their failure modes — is what lets you fix its output instead of trusting it blindly.
🎥 Watch: IBM — 'Docling' walkthrough; the Docling docs/architecture overview.
💻 Code: Run Docling on a representative document and dump the intermediate outputs (not just final JSON); identify which sub-model produced each error.

units.title: VLM architecture (encoder -> projector -> LLM)
units.text:
A vision-language model bolts a CLIP-style vision encoder to an LLM via a projector that turns image features into tokens the LLM reads (e.g. Qwen-VL, LLaVA). This is where your whole track converges: CV eyes + LLM reasoning.
🎥 Watch: Umar Jamil — 'How LLaVA / vision-language models work'; 'Qwen-VL explained'.
💻 Code: Sketch the VLM data flow (image -> encoder -> projector -> LLM tokens); run a small VLM on an image and trace where the image 'becomes' tokens.

units.title: Structured extraction, grounding & quantization
units.text:
Prompting a VLM for structured JSON, the hallucination/grounding problem (make it cite the region), and running big models small: quantization (GGUF, 4-bit) and LoRA at concept level. This is production document-AI on a budget.
🎥 Watch: 'Structured output from VLMs'; 'GGUF & 4-bit quantization explained'; 'LoRA in one video'.
💻 Code: Run a quantized VLM (e.g. Qwen2-VL-2B GGUF) to extract structured fields from documents; compare its output to Docling's; add a grounding check.

units.title: Document-AI: Docling vs a quantized VLM
units.text: [Block A] Dissect a Docling run on real documents (intermediate outputs, per-stage errors) and quantify where it wins and where it breaks. [Block B] Run a small quantized VLM (Qwen2-VL-2B GGUF) on the same documents for structured extraction; build a side-by-side comparison with a grounding/accuracy check. [Block C] Ship: a comparison report + a small extraction service, and a README mapping every OCR stage back to the CV weeks that own it — a strong document-AI capstone piece.
units.demo: Document-AI pipeline: Docling vs a quantized VLM for structured extraction, with grounding checks.

units.title: Where it all converges
units.text: OCR anatomy, classical-CV front-ends, Docling internals and VLM architecture tie the whole track to your actual work. Re-run your comparison on a fresh document and narrate the architecture file by file.
units.mastery: Map each OCR stage onto the CV weeks that own it, sketch the VLM encoder->projector->LLM flow, and say how you'd stop a VLM from hallucinating a field that isn't on the page.

units.title: Video: temporal dimension & optical flow
units.text:
Video adds time: frame sampling, temporal redundancy, and optical flow (per-pixel motion between frames). Flow is the classical motion primitive behind tracking, stabilization and action cues. The tradeoff is always accuracy vs compute-per-second.
🎥 Watch: OpenCV — 'Optical Flow'; First Principles of CV (Nayar) — 'Optical Flow'.
💻 Code: Compute dense (Farneback) and sparse (Lucas-Kanade) optical flow on a short clip; visualize the motion field; sample frames at different rates and note the tradeoff.

units.title: Video models
units.text:
Approaches to modelling time: 3D CNNs (conv over space+time), CNN+RNN, and video transformers (attention over space-time tokens). Cost grows fast, so frame sampling and clip length are real design choices.
🎥 Watch: 'Video classification: 3D CNNs vs transformers'; 'SlowFast / TimeSformer explained'.
💻 Code: Run a pretrained video-classification model on short clips; experiment with clip length and frame sampling and watch accuracy vs speed move.

units.title: 3D vision: depth, point clouds, meshes
units.text:
3D representations: depth maps (2.5D), point clouds, voxels and meshes. Point clouds have no grid, so vanilla convolution fails — PointNet's permutation-invariant fix is the classic answer. Depth estimation turns one image into geometry.
🎥 Watch: 'PointNet explained'; 'Monocular depth estimation overview'.
💻 Code: Estimate a depth map from a single image with a pretrained model; back-project to a point cloud and visualize it with Open3D.

units.title: Novel view synthesis: NeRF & Gaussian splatting
units.text:
A NeRF is a small network that IS the scene: query a 3D point + view direction, get colour + density, render by integrating along rays. 3D Gaussian splatting is its faster successor. The mind-shift: the model is the 3D asset, not a file it outputs.
🎥 Watch: Yannic Kilcher — 'NeRF'; '3D Gaussian Splatting explained'.
💻 Code: Run a small NeRF or Gaussian-splatting demo on a toy scene/images; render a novel viewpoint; note the training-time vs quality tradeoff.

units.title: Capstone framing & portfolio
units.text:
Pull the track together: scope one end-to-end vision system that's real for you (a document-understanding pipeline is the natural fit), decide the architecture from the weeks you've built, and plan a portfolio writeup that reads like an engineer's, not a tutorial's.
🎥 Watch: Revisit your own CV1-11 repos; skim two strong CV project writeups for structure.
💻 Code: Write the capstone spec: problem, data, architecture (naming which week each component comes from), evaluation, and the demo you'll ship.

units.title: Computer Vision capstone — ship an end-to-end system
units.text: [Block A] Build a real, end-to-end vision system — a document-understanding pipeline is the recommended fit: scan/deskew (CV2) -> region detect/segment (CV6/7) -> recognize/extract (CV11) with honest evaluation. [Block B] Make it usable: a demo (upload -> structured result), sensible latency on your hardware, and a metrics section that's honest about failure modes. [Block C] Ship: a polished repo + README + demo that a recruiter or professor can grasp in two minutes, and that maps each component back to the week it came from.
units.demo: End-to-end vision capstone: a document-understanding system shipped with a demo and honest evaluation.

units.title: Phase 0 review — vision, end to end
units.text: Video, 3D and the capstone close a full in-depth vision track: from pixels and classical CV through CNNs, transformers, generative and document AI. Re-read your capstone as a stranger would and cut one thing that doesn't earn its place.
units.mastery: Explain why a NeRF is a function rather than a 3D file, why a point cloud breaks a normal convolution, and give the two-minute architecture tour of your capstone.

units.title: RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs
units.text:
Modeling sequences with recurrence, the vanishing-gradient problem, and how LSTM/GRU gates fix long-range memory.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'The Unreasonable Effectiveness of RNNs' (blog); StatQuest — RNNs/LSTMs.
💻 Code: Build a character-level RNN/LSTM in PyTorch and generate text.

units.title: Word embeddings (word2vec, GloVe)
units.text:
Dense word vectors capturing meaning (king - man + woman = queen); skip-gram/CBOW and how embeddings are learned.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — 'The Illustrated Word2vec'.
💻 Code: Train word2vec on a corpus and explore analogies + nearest neighbors.

units.title: Tokenization & text preprocessing
units.text:
From text to tokens: word/subword (BPE) tokenization, normalization, and why tokenization shapes everything downstream.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'Let's build the GPT Tokenizer'; HuggingFace — tokenizers.
💻 Code: Compare word-level vs BPE tokenization on a corpus; inspect the vocab and OOV behavior.

units.title: seq2seq & attention
units.text:
Encoder-decoder for translation/summarization, and attention as the fix for the fixed-context bottleneck — the bridge to Transformers.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — 'Visualizing seq2seq with attention'; Stanford CS224N — attention.
💻 Code: Build a small seq2seq model with attention for a toy translation/copy task.

units.title: Classic NLP tasks
units.text:
Text classification, NER, sentiment and NLP evaluation — the tasks LLMs now subsume but you should understand.
🎥 Watch: HuggingFace NLP course (early chapters); CS224N.
💻 Code: Build a text classifier (embeddings + a small net) and evaluate it properly.

units.title: Text classifier / seq2seq model
units.text: [Block A] Build a solid text model: a classifier (embeddings -> net) or a seq2seq-with-attention for a small task. [Block B] Add proper tokenization, training, and NLP-appropriate evaluation. [Block C] Write up how attention solved the seq2seq bottleneck — the perfect setup for next week's Transformers.

units.title: Modeling sequences
units.text: RNNs/LSTMs, embeddings, tokenization, seq2seq + attention and classic NLP are the pre-Transformer world — and attention is the thread into it. Re-read the Illustrated Word2vec.
units.mastery: Why do RNNs struggle with long sequences, and what problem does attention solve in seq2seq?

units.title: The attention mechanism, deep
units.text:
You met attention building a Vision Transformer in the CV track; here it's the engine of language. Query/key/value attention: every token attends to every other, weighted by relevance — now applied to text, causal masking, and the scale that makes LLMs work.
🎥 Watch: 3Blue1Brown — attention; Jay Alammar — 'The Illustrated Transformer'.
💻 Code: Implement scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask from scratch in PyTorch; verify shapes/softmax and that the mask blocks future tokens.

units.title: The Transformer: encoder / decoder
units.text:
The full architecture: multi-head attention, feed-forward blocks, residual connections + layernorm, encoder vs decoder stacks.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — Illustrated Transformer; skim 'Attention Is All You Need'.
💻 Code: Assemble a single Transformer block (attention + FFN + residual + norm) in PyTorch.

units.title: Self-attention, multi-head, positional encoding
units.text:
Multiple heads capture different relations; positional encodings inject order into an otherwise order-blind mechanism.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'Let's build GPT' (self-attention section).
💻 Code: Add multi-head attention + positional encodings to your block and visualize an attention matrix.

units.title: BERT vs GPT families
units.text:
Encoder-only (BERT, bidirectional, understanding) vs decoder-only (GPT, autoregressive, generation) vs encoder-decoder (T5) — and what each is for.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — 'The Illustrated GPT-2' and 'Illustrated BERT'.
💻 Code: Load BERT and GPT-2 from HuggingFace and compare what each does on the same text.

units.title: Building a transformer block
units.text:
Putting it together into a working decoder-only LM: embeddings, N blocks, a head, and the training objective.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'Let's build GPT: from scratch'.
💻 Code: Wire embeddings + stacked blocks + an output head into a tiny GPT and do a forward pass.

units.title: Transformer from scratch (nanoGPT-style)
units.text: [Block A] Build a decoder-only Transformer (GPT) from scratch in PyTorch following Karpathy's 'Let's build GPT': attention, blocks, positional encodings. [Block B] Train it on a text corpus (tiny-shakespeare or your own) and generate samples. [Block C] Annotate every component with what it does + why; publish a 'built a GPT from scratch' repo — a flagship AI project.
units.demo: GPT / Transformer implemented from scratch in PyTorch (nanoGPT-style).

units.title: Attention is the engine
units.text: Attention, the full Transformer, multi-head + positions, the BERT/GPT split and a working block are the foundation of everything modern in AI. Re-watch Karpathy's GPT build.
units.mastery: Explain self-attention with Q/K/V in one paragraph, and why positional encodings are necessary.

units.title: Pretraining objectives (MLM, CLM)
units.text:
Masked language modeling (BERT) vs causal/next-token (GPT); how self-supervised pretraining learns from raw text at scale.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — Illustrated BERT; search 'MLM vs CLM pretraining'.
💻 Code: Implement next-token (causal) training for your nanoGPT and track the loss.

units.title: Tokenizers: BPE & SentencePiece
units.text:
Byte-pair encoding and SentencePiece: how subword vocabularies are built, and their effect on cost and multilinguality.
🎥 Watch: Karpathy — 'Let's build the GPT Tokenizer'; HuggingFace tokenizers.
💻 Code: Train a BPE tokenizer on your corpus and plug it into your GPT.

units.title: Scaling laws & model families
units.text:
How loss scales with params/data/compute (Chinchilla), and the landscape of open vs closed model families.
🎥 Watch: Search 'scaling laws Chinchilla explained'.
💻 Code: Train your small GPT at 2-3 sizes and plot loss vs params/compute — see scaling firsthand.

units.title: The HuggingFace ecosystem
units.text:
transformers, datasets, tokenizers and the Hub; loading, running and sharing pretrained models the standard way.
🎥 Watch: HuggingFace — NLP course (using Transformers).
💻 Code: Load a pretrained model + tokenizer from the Hub, run inference, and push a model/dataset.

units.title: Fine-tuning basics
units.text:
Full fine-tuning a pretrained model on a downstream task, and the train/eval loop with the HuggingFace Trainer.
🎥 Watch: HuggingFace — fine-tuning a pretrained model.
💻 Code: Fine-tune a small pretrained model (e.g. DistilBERT) on a classification task with Trainer.

units.title: Train a small GPT on a custom corpus
units.text: [Block A] Take your nanoGPT, add a trained BPE tokenizer and causal pretraining, and train on a corpus you care about. [Block B] Scale it up a little, add eval (perplexity) and sampling controls (temperature/top-k). [Block C] Write up the pretraining run + scaling observations — deep, credible AI portfolio content.
units.demo: Trained a small GPT from scratch on a custom corpus (tokenizer, training loop, sampling).

units.title: How LLMs are made
units.text: Pretraining objectives, tokenizers, scaling laws, the HuggingFace ecosystem and fine-tuning basics are how raw text becomes a language model. Re-read your loss/perplexity curves.
units.mastery: Contrast MLM and causal pretraining, and what scaling laws say about spending compute on params vs data.

units.title: Inference, sampling & decoding
units.text:
How an LLM generates: logits -> sampling (greedy, temperature, top-k, top-p), and why decoding settings change outputs.
🎥 Watch: Search 'LLM sampling temperature top-p explained'.
💻 Code: Take a HuggingFace LLM and generate with different decoding settings; observe the effect.

units.title: Prompting techniques
units.text:
Zero/few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured prompts, and system/user roles — reliable behavior from a fixed model.
🎥 Watch: Search 'prompt engineering guide'; Anthropic prompt-engineering docs.
💻 Code: Take a task and improve results measurably by iterating prompts (zero-shot -> few-shot -> CoT).

units.title: Context, tokens & cost
units.text:
Context windows, tokenization cost, managing long inputs (truncation, chunking), and latency/price tradeoffs.
🎥 Watch: Search 'LLM context window tokens explained'.
💻 Code: Measure tokens + cost for prompts of different sizes and build a token budget for an app.

units.title: LLM APIs & the ecosystem
units.text:
Calling LLM APIs (messages, system prompts, streaming, tools), and the open-vs-hosted landscape.
🎥 Watch: Read a major provider's messages/API docs (e.g. Anthropic/OpenAI).
💻 Code: Build a small app that calls an LLM API with a system prompt and streams the response.

units.title: LLM evaluation
units.text:
Why eval is hard, and approaches: golden sets, rubric/LLM-as-judge, and task-specific metrics — eval-driven development.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen — evaluating LLM apps; search 'LLM evaluation methods'.
💻 Code: Build a small eval harness (golden examples + an LLM-as-judge rubric) for a task.

units.title: LLM app with strong prompting + an eval harness
units.text: [Block A] Build a real LLM feature (summarizer, extractor, assistant) via an API with a solid system prompt. [Block B] Add structured output, error handling, streaming and a token/cost budget. [Block C] Build an eval harness (golden set + LLM-judge) and iterate prompts against it — eval-driven, portfolio-grade.

units.title: Using LLMs well
units.text: Decoding, prompting, context/cost, APIs and evaluation are the practical foundation of building with LLMs. Re-read your eval results.
units.mastery: How does temperature/top-p change generation, and why is a golden-set + judge eval better than eyeballing outputs?

units.title: Embeddings, deep
units.text:
Text embeddings map meaning to vectors; similarity search, and choosing/measuring an embedding model.
🎥 Watch: Jay Alammar — illustrated embeddings; search 'text embeddings explained'.
💻 Code: Embed a corpus with an embedding model and build semantic search over it (cosine similarity).

units.title: Vector databases (pgvector, etc.)
units.text:
Storing + searching embeddings at scale: ANN indexes (HNSW) and pgvector/FAISS/other stores.
🎥 Watch: Search 'vector database explained'; pgvector docs.
💻 Code: Load embeddings into pgvector (or FAISS) and run fast approximate nearest-neighbor search.

units.title: RAG architecture
units.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve relevant chunks, put them in the prompt, generate a grounded answer — the dominant enterprise LLM pattern.
🎥 Watch: Search 'RAG explained'; Chip Huyen / Anthropic on RAG.
💻 Code: Build a minimal RAG: chunk -> embed -> retrieve -> prompt -> answer over your own docs.

units.title: Chunking, retrieval & reranking
units.text:
Chunking strategies, hybrid search (keyword + vector), reranking and query rewriting — where RAG quality is won or lost.
🎥 Watch: Search 'RAG chunking strategies reranking'.
💻 Code: Improve your RAG's retrieval with better chunking + a reranker; measure the answer-quality lift.

units.title: RAG evaluation
units.text:
Evaluating RAG: retrieval metrics (recall/precision@k) + answer faithfulness/groundedness (RAGAS-style).
🎥 Watch: Search 'RAG evaluation RAGAS'.
💻 Code: Build a RAG eval set and score retrieval + faithfulness; find and fix the weakest link.

units.title: Production RAG over your own corpus
units.text: [Block A] Build a real RAG system over a corpus you care about (your notes, docs, a codebase): ingest -> chunk -> embed -> vector store. [Block B] Add hybrid retrieval + reranking, query rewriting, citations, and a chat UI/API. [Block C] Add a RAG eval harness (retrieval + faithfulness) and iterate; ship it — a flagship AI portfolio project.
units.demo: Production RAG over a real corpus: hybrid retrieval, reranking, citations, eval harness.

units.title: Grounding LLMs in data
units.text: Embeddings, vector DBs, the RAG loop, chunking/reranking and RAG eval are the most in-demand LLM skill set right now. Re-read your RAG eval scores.
units.mastery: Walk through a RAG query end to end, and name the two places retrieval quality most often breaks.

units.title: Full fine-tuning, LoRA, QLoRA
units.text:
When to fine-tune, full vs parameter-efficient (LoRA freezes the model and trains small adapters; QLoRA adds quantization).
🎥 Watch: Sebastian Raschka — LoRA/fine-tuning; search 'LoRA QLoRA explained'.
💻 Code: Fine-tune a small open model with LoRA (PEFT) on a task dataset.

units.title: PEFT & adapters
units.text:
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, adapters, prefix/prompt tuning) — big gains, tiny trainable footprints.
🎥 Watch: HuggingFace PEFT docs; Sebastian Raschka.
💻 Code: Compare LoRA rank / target-module choices and their effect on quality + trainable params.

units.title: Instruction tuning; RLHF/DPO intuition
units.text:
