Turning a base model into an assistant: instruction tuning, and preference alignment (RLHF, DPO) at an intuition level.
🎥 Watch: Search 'RLHF explained' and 'DPO direct preference optimization'.
💻 Code: Instruction-tune a small model on an instruction dataset and compare to the base model.

units.title: Quantization & distillation
units.text:
Shrinking models for cheaper inference: quantization (int8/int4, GGUF) and distillation (a small model learns from a big one).
🎥 Watch: Search 'LLM quantization explained GGUF' and 'knowledge distillation'.
💻 Code: Quantize your fine-tuned model to int4 and measure the size/latency vs quality tradeoff.

units.title: When to tune vs RAG vs prompt
units.text:
The decision framework: prompting for behavior, RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for style/format/skill — and their costs.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen; search 'fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting'.
💻 Code: Take one task and solve it three ways (prompt, RAG, fine-tune); compare quality, cost and effort.

units.title: Fine-tune an open LLM with LoRA
units.text: [Block A] Pick a task where fine-tuning helps (style, format, a domain skill) and prepare a clean instruction dataset. [Block B] Fine-tune an open model with LoRA/QLoRA; evaluate against the base model + a prompted baseline. [Block C] Quantize + serve it, and write up the tune-vs-RAG-vs-prompt decision — a strong applied-AI portfolio piece.
units.demo: Fine-tuned an open LLM with LoRA/QLoRA and served it.

units.title: Adapting models to you
units.text: Full vs PEFT fine-tuning, instruction tuning/alignment, quantization/distillation and the tune-vs-RAG-vs-prompt decision are how you shape models. Re-read your three-way comparison.
units.mastery: How does LoRA fine-tune a model without touching most of its weights, and when do you fine-tune instead of RAG?

units.title: Agent concepts: ReAct & planning
units.text:
Agents = an LLM + tools + a loop; ReAct (reason + act), planning, and the reason-act-observe cycle.
🎥 Watch: Search 'ReAct agents explained'; Anthropic — 'Building effective agents'.
💻 Code: Build a minimal ReAct loop by hand (no framework): reason -> call a tool -> observe -> repeat.

units.title: Tool use & function calling
units.text:
Giving models tools via function/tool calling: schemas, the call loop, and parsing/validating tool outputs.
🎥 Watch: A provider's tool-use/function-calling docs (Anthropic/OpenAI).
💻 Code: Give your agent 2-3 real tools (search, calculator, an API) via function calling and let it use them.

units.title: Frameworks vs framework-light
units.text:
LangChain/LlamaIndex/LangGraph vs writing it yourself; why framework-light is often better for control and debugging.
🎥 Watch: Anthropic — 'Building effective agents' (the framework caution); search 'do you need langchain'.
💻 Code: Rebuild your agent both with a framework and framework-light; compare control and debuggability.

units.title: Memory & state
units.text:
Short-term (context) vs long-term memory (a vector store), conversation state and scratchpads.
🎥 Watch: Search 'agent memory patterns'.
💻 Code: Add long-term memory (a vector store the agent reads/writes) so it recalls past interactions.

units.title: Multi-agent systems
units.text:
When multiple specialized agents beat one (orchestrator/worker, debate, review), and the coordination cost.
🎥 Watch: Anthropic; search 'multi-agent systems LLM'.
💻 Code: Build a 2-agent setup (a worker + a reviewer/critic) and show it beats a single agent on a task.

units.title: Tool-using agent for a real task (fleet-style)
units.text: [Block A] Build an agent that does a genuinely useful task with tools (like your own bot fleet): define the tools + the loop, framework-light. [Block B] Add memory, error handling and guardrails; make it reliable, not a demo. [Block C] Deploy it (a scheduled job or a bot) and document the design — a flagship, on-brand AI portfolio project.
units.demo: Autonomous tool-using agent (framework-light) that completes a real task.

units.title: Agents that act
units.text: ReAct + planning, tool use, framework choices, memory and multi-agent patterns are how LLMs do things, not just talk. Re-read Anthropic's 'Building effective agents'.
units.mastery: Describe the reason-act-observe loop, and when a multi-agent design actually beats a single well-prompted agent.

units.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol), deep
units.text:
MCP standardizes how models connect to tools/data (servers expose tools/resources/prompts) — the 'USB-C for AI tools'.
🎥 Watch: modelcontextprotocol.io docs; search 'Model Context Protocol explained'.
💻 Code: Read the MCP spec and run an existing MCP server with a client.

units.title: Building MCP servers
units.text:
Writing an MCP server that exposes tools + resources so any MCP client (Claude, IDEs) can use your data/actions.
🎥 Watch: MCP docs — build a server (Python/TS SDK).
💻 Code: Build an MCP server exposing 2-3 tools over your data (e.g. your data platform) and connect a client.

units.title: Agent-orchestration patterns
units.text:
Orchestrator/worker, routing, chaining and evaluator-optimizer loops — deterministic control around non-deterministic models.
🎥 Watch: Anthropic — 'Building effective agents' (patterns).
💻 Code: Implement an orchestrator that routes a task to the right tool/sub-agent deterministically.

units.title: Evaluation & guardrails
units.text:
Evaluating agents (task success, trajectory), and guardrails: input/output validation, allow-lists and human-in-the-loop.
🎥 Watch: Search 'evaluating AI agents'; guardrails frameworks.
💻 Code: Add guardrails (a tool allow-list, output validation) + a task-success eval to your agent.

units.title: Cost, latency & reliability
units.text:
Agents are expensive and flaky by default: caching, step limits, retries, and cost/latency budgets.
🎥 Watch: Search 'production AI agents reliability cost'.
💻 Code: Add step limits, caching and retries; measure and cut your agent's cost per task.

units.title: MCP server + agent over your data platform
units.text: [Block A] Build an MCP server that exposes your Data-Engineering platform (query data, check pipeline status) as tools. [Block B] Build an agent that uses it to answer real questions / do real tasks, with orchestration + guardrails. [Block C] Add evaluation + cost controls and document it — this ties your DE, AI and infra work into one showcase.
units.demo: MCP server + agent exposing a data platform as LLM tools.

units.title: Wiring agents to tools
units.text: MCP, building servers, orchestration patterns, evaluation/guardrails and cost/reliability are how agents become dependable products. Re-read your guardrails.
units.mastery: What problem does MCP standardize, and what are the three things that keep a production agent reliable and affordable?

units.title: Serving LLMs (vLLM, TGI)
units.text:
Efficient LLM serving with vLLM/TGI: continuous batching, paged attention, and why naive serving is slow and expensive.
🎥 Watch: Search 'vLLM paged attention'; the vLLM docs.
💻 Code: Serve an open model with vLLM and benchmark throughput vs a naive HuggingFace pipeline.

units.title: Inference optimization: KV cache, batching
units.text:
The KV cache, continuous batching, quantization and speculative decoding — the levers of fast, cheap inference.
🎥 Watch: Search 'KV cache explained' and 'continuous batching LLM'.
💻 Code: Measure the effect of the KV cache + batching on latency/throughput for your served model.

units.title: Observability: tracing & evals
units.text:
Tracing LLM apps (spans, tokens, cost), online evals, and catching quality regressions in production.
🎥 Watch: Search 'LLM observability tracing' (LangSmith/Langfuse concepts).
💻 Code: Add tracing (tokens, latency, cost per request) + an online eval to an LLM app.

units.title: Guardrails & prompt-injection defense
units.text:
Prompt injection, jailbreaks, and defenses: input/output filtering, allow-lists, and untrusted-content isolation.
🎥 Watch: Search 'prompt injection explained'; the OWASP LLM Top 10.
💻 Code: Attack your own LLM app with prompt injection, then add defenses and re-test.

units.title: Cost at scale
units.text:
Token economics, caching, model routing (small model first) and batching — running AI affordably.
🎥 Watch: Search 'LLM cost optimization strategies'.
💻 Code: Add a cache + model-routing (cheap model first, escalate) to an app and measure the cost drop.

units.title: Deploy an LLM app with evals + guardrails
units.text: [Block A] Take your RAG/agent app and deploy it properly (vLLM or an API) with schemas + streaming. [Block B] Add observability (tracing, cost), online evals, and guardrails (injection defense, output validation). [Block C] Load-test it, add cost controls, and document the LLMOps setup — a portfolio production-AI piece.

units.title: Operating AI in production
units.text: Serving, inference optimization, observability, guardrails and cost control separate an AI demo from an AI product. Re-run your injection tests.
units.mastery: What does continuous batching + a KV cache do for LLM serving, and how do you defend against prompt injection?

units.title: Multimodal AI in practice
units.text:
You built the internals — CLIP, VLM architecture, diffusion — in the Computer Vision track; here you wire multimodal models into products: vision-language models (Qwen-VL, GPT-4V-class) for document QA, image+text search, and picking actions from a screenshot. The engineering is prompting, grounding and cost, not architecture.
🎥 Watch: Search 'building with vision-language models'; 'multimodal LLM applications'.
💻 Code: Use a VLM API/local model to answer questions over your own images/documents and build a small image+text semantic search.

units.title: Efficient architectures & long context
units.text:
Past quadratic attention: FlashAttention (identical math, IO-aware, far faster/cheaper) and state-space models (Mamba) that scale linearly with sequence length. Why 2026 cares: long-context and cheap inference. The frontier of 'attention is all you need — but can we make it cheaper?'.
🎥 Watch: 'FlashAttention explained'; 'Mamba / state-space models explained'.
💻 Code: Benchmark attention vs a linear-time alternative on growing sequence lengths; chart the memory/latency curves and explain the crossover.

units.title: Structured generation & function calling
units.text:
Constraining LLM output to schemas/JSON/grammars for reliable downstream use.
🎥 Watch: Search 'structured output LLM json schema' (outlines/instructor).
💻 Code: Force reliable JSON output from an LLM with a schema and validate it.

units.title: Knowledge graphs + LLMs
units.text:
Combining structured knowledge (graphs) with LLMs (GraphRAG) for grounded, multi-hop reasoning.
🎥 Watch: Search 'GraphRAG explained'.
💻 Code: Build a tiny knowledge graph and use it to ground/augment LLM answers (GraphRAG-lite).

units.title: Frontier reading
units.text:
Staying current: reading papers (arXiv, Papers with Code), model releases, and separating signal from hype.
🎥 Watch: Search 'how to read ML papers'.
💻 Code: Read one recent influential paper and write a one-page summary + how you'd use it.

units.title: GraphRAG system (knowledge graph + LLM)
units.text: [Block A] Extract a knowledge graph from a real corpus (entities + relations), then build GraphRAG retrieval that walks the graph for multi-hop, grounded answers with citations. [Block B] Evaluate head-to-head against vanilla vector RAG on multi-hop questions where flat retrieval fails; add structured (schema-constrained) output. [Block C] Ship: a GraphRAG service + a writeup on exactly when graph-structured retrieval beats plain RAG — a distinctive, grounded-reasoning portfolio piece.
units.demo: GraphRAG system: knowledge graph + LLM for grounded, multi-hop QA, benchmarked against vanilla RAG.

units.title: The expanding frontier
units.text: Multimodal-in-practice, efficient architectures, structured generation, KG+LLM and paper-reading keep you current as the field moves. Re-read your paper summary.
units.mastery: When does GraphRAG beat vanilla RAG, and what problem do state-space models solve that quadratic attention can't?

units.title: AI product design & UX
units.text:
Designing AI products around model strengths/weaknesses: managing uncertainty, latency, and setting user expectations.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen — AI Engineering; search 'designing AI product UX'.
💻 Code: Redesign an existing feature as an AI feature, explicitly handling errors/uncertainty in the UX.

units.title: Evaluation-driven development
units.text:
Building AI features test-first: define evals, iterate against them, and treat evals as the spec.
🎥 Watch: Chip Huyen — evaluation; search 'eval driven development LLM'.
💻 Code: For a feature, write the eval set first, then build until it passes — eval-driven.

units.title: Data flywheels
units.text:
Using production data (feedback, corrections) to continuously improve the system — the moat of AI products.
🎥 Watch: Search 'data flywheel AI product'.
💻 Code: Add a feedback-capture loop to an app that logs corrections for future improvement.

units.title: Hybrid systems (classical + LLM)
units.text:
Combining deterministic code/classical ML with LLMs — using each where it's strong (cheap/reliable vs flexible).
🎥 Watch: Search 'hybrid AI systems classical ML LLM'.
💻 Code: Build a hybrid: a cheap classifier/rules router that only calls the LLM when needed.

units.title: Case studies
units.text:
Studying real AI products (how they use retrieval, evals, guardrails, feedback) to build product judgment.
🎥 Watch: Read engineering blogs (Anthropic and others) on shipped AI features.
💻 Code: Reverse-engineer a shipped AI product into an architecture + tradeoffs writeup.

units.title: Ship a polished AI product feature
units.text: [Block A] Build a genuinely useful, polished AI feature end to end (not a demo): clear UX, error handling, evals. [Block B] Make it a hybrid where sensible (classical + LLM) and add a feedback/data-flywheel loop. [Block C] Deploy it with observability + guardrails and write the product case study — portfolio-grade AI engineering.

units.title: Building AI products
units.text: Product design, eval-driven development, data flywheels, hybrid systems and case studies are what AI engineering actually is. Re-read your case study.
units.mastery: Why is eval-driven development the right way to build with LLMs, and where should classical code do the work instead of the model?

units.title: Architecture & data
units.text:
Scope an ambitious AI system; design the architecture (retrieval/agent/model) and assemble the data/knowledge.
🎥 Watch: Reuse Chip Huyen + Anthropic agent patterns.
💻 Code: Write the AI-system design doc + architecture diagram and prepare the data/corpus.

units.title: Retrieval / agent layer
units.text:
Build the core intelligence: RAG and/or an agent with tools over your data.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your RAG + agent work.
💻 Code: Build the retrieval/agent layer with the right tools + memory.

units.title: Model integration
units.text:
Wire in the model(s): prompting, structured output, and fine-tuning where it helps.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your prompting/fine-tuning work.
💻 Code: Integrate the model with strong prompts/structured output; fine-tune if it earns its keep.

units.title: Evaluation harness & guardrails
units.text:
Build the eval harness (task success, faithfulness) and guardrails before you trust it.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your eval + guardrails work.
💻 Code: Build the eval harness + guardrails and iterate the system against them.

units.title: Portfolio writeup
units.text:
Deploy, add observability/cost controls, and write the case study + demo.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your LLMOps work.
💻 Code: Deploy with observability, write the case study, and record a demo.

units.title: AI-system capstone — build & ship
units.text: [Block A] Assemble an ambitious AI system (RAG + agent + tools) over real data, framework-light and reliable. [Block B] Add evals, guardrails, observability and cost controls — production-grade, not a demo. [Block C] Ship it: repo, case study, demo — your flagship AI portfolio project.
units.demo: Production AI system: RAG + agent + evals + guardrails.

units.title: Phase 3 review
units.text: You've gone from a neuron to a shipped, evaluated AI system. Step back: what's genuinely yours now, and how will the Linux/systems phase let you productionize all of it?
units.mastery: Give the 3-minute tour of your AI system: the architecture, why RAG/agent/fine-tune, how you evaluate it, and how you keep it safe and affordable. Spaced recall (cold): explain exactly-once streaming (DE), gradient boosting vs a neural net (ML), and where each fits in your AI system.

units.title: systemd: units, services, journald
units.text:
systemd runs modern Linux: unit files, services, targets, enabling/starting, and reading logs with journalctl.
🎥 Watch: Search 'systemd tutorial' and 'journalctl explained'.
💻 Code: Write a systemd service unit for your automation script; enable it and read its logs via journalctl.

units.title: Networking basics: ip, ss, DNS, curl
units.text:
Inspecting/configuring the network from the shell: ip, ss (sockets), DNS (dig), and curl for HTTP debugging.
🎥 Watch: Julia Evans — networking zines; search 'ip ss dig tutorial'.
💻 Code: Diagnose a connectivity problem with ip/ss/dig/curl and find what's listening on a port.

units.title: SSH, keys, tmux & remote work
units.text:
SSH (key-based auth, config, tunnels), tmux for persistent sessions, and safe remote workflows.
🎥 Watch: Search 'SSH keys tutorial' and 'tmux crash course'.
💻 Code: Set up key-based SSH to a server/VM, an SSH config alias, and a tmux workflow that survives disconnects.

units.title: Disks, mounts, df/du & LVM basics
units.text:
Storage admin: partitions, filesystems, mounting, df/du for space, and LVM for flexible volumes.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux disk management df du mount' and 'LVM basics'.
💻 Code: Add/mount a disk (on a VM), find what's eating space with du, and resize a logical volume.

units.title: Log management & monitoring basics
units.text:
System logs, log rotation (logrotate), and basic health monitoring (uptime, load, memory, disk).
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux logging logrotate' and system-monitoring basics.
💻 Code: Set up logrotate for your service's logs and a simple health-check script with alerting.

units.title: Provision & harden a real Linux server
units.text: [Block A] Spin up a cloud VM (or a local VM) and provision it: users, SSH keys, firewall, your service via systemd. [Block B] Harden it: disable password/root SSH, set up ufw/iptables, automatic updates and fail2ban. [Block C] Document the runbook + a from-scratch provision script — a portfolio 'I can run production Linux' piece.

units.title: Operating a Linux box
units.text: systemd, networking tools, SSH/tmux, storage and logging/monitoring are the core of running real servers. Re-check your server's hardening.
units.mastery: Walk through provisioning + hardening a fresh server, and how you'd debug 'the service won't start' with systemd + journalctl.

units.title: Process anatomy: address space, fds (/proc)
units.text:
What a process really is: the virtual address space (text/data/heap/stack), the fd table, and the PCB — all visible in /proc.
🎥 Watch: OSTEP — processes; Julia Evans — /proc.
💻 Code: Explore /proc/<pid>/ for a running process: maps, fd, status — annotate every region.

units.title: Virtual memory & paging: page tables, TLB, COW
units.text:
Every process thinks it owns all memory; page tables translate virtual->physical, the TLB caches translations, and copy-on-write makes fork() cheap.
🎥 Watch: OSTEP — virtual memory / paging.
💻 Code: Demonstrate copy-on-write: fork a process that allocated a large array and watch RSS stay shared until a write.

units.title: The page cache, dirty pages & writeback
units.text:
Free RAM isn't wasted: the kernel caches file pages (why the second read is instant); dirty pages + writeback.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux page cache explained'; Brendan Gregg.
💻 Code: Show the page cache: time a cold vs warm read of a big file; drop_caches and repeat.

units.title: Syscalls & the user/kernel boundary (strace)
units.text:
A syscall is a formal request across a security boundary (a mode switch); strace shows every one a process makes.
🎥 Watch: Julia Evans — strace zine; search 'Linux syscalls explained'.
💻 Code: strace a real program (e.g. one of your bots) and explain the syscall pattern you see.

units.title: Signals, zombies & the process lifecycle
units.text:
fork/exec/wait, signals (how processes are interrupted/terminated), and zombies/orphans.
🎥 Watch: OSTEP — process API; Julia Evans — signals.
💻 Code: Write a program that handles signals gracefully, and create (then reap) a zombie to understand it.

units.title: Process & memory instrumentation toolkit
units.text: [Block A] Build a tool that, given a PID, reports its memory map (/proc/pid/maps), open fds, and live RSS/threads. [Block B] Add a strace-lite mode (ptrace or parse strace) that summarizes the syscalls a process makes. [Block C] Run it against your own agent fleet and write up what you learned — a standout systems portfolio project.

units.title: What a process really is
units.text: The address space + /proc, virtual memory/paging, the page cache, syscalls/strace and the process lifecycle are how programs actually run. Re-read one process's /proc.
units.mastery: Trace what happens from fork() to a running program, and why copy-on-write makes forking a 4GB process instant.

units.title: Filesystems, the VFS & inodes
units.text:
How files are stored: inodes vs names (hard/soft links), the VFS abstraction over ext4/xfs, and directories as data.
🎥 Watch: OSTEP — file systems; Julia Evans — inodes.
💻 Code: Explore inodes: create hard/soft links, delete the original, and explain what survives and why.

units.title: File I/O: buffered vs direct, fsync, mmap
units.text:
How reads/writes actually hit disk: buffering, fsync for durability, O_DIRECT, and mmap for memory-mapped files.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux file IO buffered direct fsync'; OSTEP.
💻 Code: Compare throughput of buffered vs fsync-per-write vs mmap for writing a large file.

units.title: The CPU scheduler (CFS), context switches
units.text:
How Linux shares CPUs: the Completely Fair Scheduler, nice/priorities, and the cost of context switches.
🎥 Watch: OSTEP — scheduling; Brendan Gregg — scheduler.
💻 Code: Observe scheduling: run CPU-bound tasks, change nice values, and measure context switches with vmstat/pidstat.

units.title: epoll & non-blocking I/O
units.text:
How servers handle thousands of connections: blocking vs non-blocking I/O and epoll (the engine under async runtimes).
🎥 Watch: Search 'epoll explained' and 'C10k problem'.
💻 Code: Write a tiny epoll-based echo server that handles many concurrent connections in one thread.

units.title: Capabilities & security primitives
units.text:
Fine-grained privileges (capabilities) beyond root, plus seccomp and namespaces as security building blocks (a bridge to containers).
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux capabilities explained' and 'seccomp'.
💻 Code: Drop capabilities from a process and grant just one (e.g. bind a low port) instead of full root.

units.title: Mini shell / high-throughput I/O tool
units.text: [Block A] Build a small Unix shell (C/Python): fork/exec, pipes, redirection and job control — using the syscalls directly. [Block B] Or build a high-throughput I/O tool (an epoll server or a parallel file processor) and benchmark it. [Block C] Write up the syscalls involved and the performance numbers — a deep systems portfolio piece.

units.title: How the kernel schedules & serves I/O
units.text: Filesystems/inodes, file I/O, the scheduler, epoll and capabilities are the kernel services every program relies on. Re-read your I/O benchmark.
units.mastery: Explain the difference between a hard and soft link at the inode level, and how epoll lets one thread serve thousands of connections.

units.title: The network stack & sockets (ss, ip)
units.text:
The layered stack (L2-L7), how a socket connects an app to the network, and inspecting it with ss/ip.
🎥 Watch: Julia Evans — networking zines; search 'Linux network stack explained'.
💻 Code: Map a live connection through the stack; use ss to see every socket and its state.

units.title: TCP deep: handshake, congestion control
units.text:
The 3-way handshake, flow + congestion control, TIME_WAIT, and why TCP behaves the way it does.
🎥 Watch: Search 'TCP handshake congestion control explained'; Julia Evans.
💻 Code: Watch a TCP handshake + teardown in tcpdump/Wireshark and identify each packet.

units.title: DNS, TLS, HTTP/1.1 -> HTTP/3
units.text:
How a URL becomes a response: DNS resolution, the TLS handshake, and HTTP/1.1 -> 2 -> 3 (QUIC).
🎥 Watch: Julia Evans — DNS/TLS zines; search 'HTTP/2 HTTP/3 explained'.
💻 Code: Trace a full request: dig the DNS, inspect the TLS handshake (openssl s_client), compare HTTP/1.1 vs 2.

units.title: tcpdump / Wireshark
units.text:
Packet capture and analysis — the ultimate 'what's actually on the wire' debugging tool.
🎥 Watch: Search 'tcpdump tutorial' and 'Wireshark crash course'.
💻 Code: Capture and dissect a real app's traffic; find a specific request/response in the capture.

units.title: Network tuning & throughput
units.text:
Bandwidth vs latency, buffer sizes, and diagnosing slow networks — it matters for distributed data/ML systems.
🎥 Watch: Brendan Gregg — network performance; search 'Linux network tuning'.
💻 Code: Measure throughput/latency (iperf, ping) between hosts and tune a buffer or MTU setting.

units.title: TCP proxy / load balancer + packet analysis
units.text: [Block A] Build a TCP proxy (accept -> connect upstream -> pipe both ways) using sockets; handle many connections. [Block B] Turn it into a simple load balancer (round-robin across backends) with health checks. [Block C] Analyze its traffic in Wireshark and write up the request journey + your L4 LB design — a flagship networking project.

units.title: A request's full journey
units.text: The stack/sockets, TCP internals, DNS/TLS/HTTP, packet analysis and tuning explain every request your systems make. Re-read your Wireshark capture.
units.mastery: Walk a request from URL to response through DNS, TLS, TCP and HTTP, and what tcpdump would show at each step.

units.title: Namespaces — the isolation primitives
units.text:
The Linux namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) that give a container its own view of the system — half of what a container is.
🎥 Watch: Liz Rice — 'Containers from scratch'; search 'Linux namespaces explained'.
💻 Code: Use unshare to create a process in its own PID + mount namespace and observe the isolation.

units.title: cgroups — resource limits & accounting
units.text:
Control groups that limit and account CPU/memory/IO — the other half of a container; cgroups v2.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux cgroups explained'; Liz Rice.
💻 Code: Put a process in a cgroup with a memory + CPU limit and watch it get throttled/OOM-killed.

units.title: Docker internals: layers, union fs
units.text:
How Docker images work: layered union filesystems (overlayfs), the build cache, and image vs container.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Docker images layers overlayfs explained'; TechWorld with Nana — Docker.
💻 Code: Inspect an image's layers, write an efficient multi-stage Dockerfile, and minimize image size.

units.title: Container networking & volumes
units.text:
How containers get networking (bridge, veth, port mapping) and persistent storage (volumes, bind mounts).
🎥 Watch: Search 'Docker networking explained' and 'Docker volumes'.
💻 Code: Connect two containers over a user-defined network and persist data with a volume.

units.title: Image build & supply-chain security
units.text:
Building minimal, secure images: distroless/scratch, non-root users, vulnerability scanning and signing.
🎥 Watch: Search 'container image security best practices' and 'distroless images'.
💻 Code: Harden a Dockerfile (non-root, minimal base, scan with trivy) and shrink + secure the image.

units.title: Container runtime from scratch
units.text: [Block A] Build a minimal container runtime (Go/Python) using namespaces + cgroups + chroot/pivot_root — the 'Docker in 100 lines' project. [Block B] Add a limited rootfs image and resource limits; run a real command inside it. [Block C] Write up 'what a container actually is' with your code — a flagship, deeply-credible systems portfolio project.
units.demo: Container runtime built from scratch (namespaces + cgroups + rootfs).

units.title: How containers really work
units.text: Namespaces, cgroups, Docker internals, container networking and image security show a container is just Linux primitives, not magic. Re-read your runtime code.
units.mastery: Explain a container as namespaces + cgroups + a rootfs, and what each namespace isolates.

units.title: Architecture: control plane, kubelet
units.text:
The K8s architecture: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager (control plane) and the kubelet on each node.
🎥 Watch: TechWorld with Nana — Kubernetes crash course; search 'Kubernetes architecture explained'.
💻 Code: Stand up a local cluster (kind/minikube) and inspect the control-plane components.

units.title: Pods, services, deployments, config
units.text:
The core objects: pods, deployments (rollouts/replicas), services (networking) and ConfigMaps/Secrets.
🎥 Watch: TechWorld with Nana — K8s objects; the Kubernetes docs tutorials.
💻 Code: Deploy an app: Deployment + Service + ConfigMap; scale it and do a rolling update.

units.title: Scheduling, resources & autoscaling
units.text:
How pods get placed (requests/limits, affinity, taints), and autoscaling (HPA) based on load.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Kubernetes scheduling requests limits HPA'.
💻 Code: Set resource requests/limits, add a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, and load-test the scaling.

units.title: Operators & CRDs
units.text:
Extending K8s with CRDs and operators that encode operational knowledge (the pattern behind data/ML platforms on K8s).
🎥 Watch: Search 'Kubernetes operators CRD explained'.
💻 Code: Install an operator (e.g. Prometheus/Postgres) via a CRD and use its custom resources.

units.title: GPU scheduling for inference
units.text:
Running GPU workloads on K8s: device plugins, requesting GPUs, and scheduling inference/training — ties back to your AI phase.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Kubernetes GPU scheduling device plugin'.
💻 Code: Schedule a pod that requests a GPU (or simulate with resource classes) and serve a model on it.

units.title: Deploy & operate an app on K8s (Helm)
units.text: [Block A] Package a real app (your RAG/agent or ML API) as a Helm chart: Deployment, Service, ConfigMap/Secret, HPA. [Block B] Deploy to a cluster with health checks, resource limits, autoscaling and a rolling-update strategy. [Block C] Add an ingress + TLS and document the operations runbook — a portfolio 'I can run K8s' piece.

units.title: Orchestration at scale
units.text: The control plane, core objects, scheduling/autoscaling, operators/CRDs and GPU scheduling are how you run containers in production at scale. Re-read your Helm chart.
units.mastery: Trace what happens from 'kubectl apply' to a running pod, and how a Service + Deployment give you self-healing scale.

units.title: Terraform, deep
units.text:
Declarative infrastructure with Terraform: providers, resources, state, plan/apply, and modules for reuse.
🎥 Watch: TechWorld with Nana — Terraform; HashiCorp Learn.
💻 Code: Provision real cloud infra (a VM + network + a managed DB) with Terraform using variables + a module.

units.title: Ansible & configuration management
units.text:
Configuring servers idempotently with Ansible (playbooks, roles, inventory) — the config half of IaC.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Ansible tutorial'; TechWorld with Nana.
💻 Code: Write an Ansible playbook that provisions + hardens a server (reuse your server-provisioning + hardening work) idempotently.

units.title: GitOps with ArgoCD / Flux
units.text:
GitOps: git as the single source of truth, with ArgoCD/Flux continuously reconciling the cluster to match.
🎥 Watch: Search 'GitOps explained ArgoCD'; TechWorld with Nana.
💻 Code: Set up ArgoCD to auto-deploy your Helm app from git; change git and watch it reconcile.

units.title: Helm & templating
units.text:
Helm for templated, versioned K8s deployments: charts, values, releases and rollbacks.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Helm tutorial'.
💻 Code: Parameterize your chart with values for dev/prod and practice a release + rollback.

units.title: Secrets management (Vault, SOPS)
units.text:
Handling secrets safely in IaC/GitOps: Vault, sealed-secrets/SOPS, and never committing plaintext.
🎥 Watch: Search 'secrets management Kubernetes Vault SOPS'.
💻 Code: Encrypt secrets with SOPS (or sealed-secrets) so they can live in git safely, and wire them into a deploy.

units.title: Full IaC + GitOps for your platform
units.text: [Block A] Define your whole stack as code: Terraform for cloud infra (cluster, DB, networking), versioned + modular. [Block B] Deploy apps via GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux) from git, with Helm charts and encrypted secrets. [Block C] Make it fully reproducible ('git clone -> apply -> running platform') and document it — a flagship infra portfolio piece.
units.demo: Infrastructure-as-code + GitOps: Terraform + ArgoCD, reproducible from git.

units.title: Infrastructure as code
units.text: Terraform, Ansible, GitOps, Helm and secrets management turn infrastructure into versioned, reviewable, reproducible code. Re-run your apply from scratch.
units.mastery: What does GitOps give you over 'kubectl apply by hand', and how do you keep secrets in git without leaking them?

units.title: Azure fundamentals & the resource model
units.text:
Azure's hierarchy — tenant -> subscription -> resource group -> resource — with Azure Resource Manager (ARM) as the control plane and tags on everything. Regions and availability zones decide resilience. This mental model comes before any single service.
🎥 Watch: John Savill's Technical Training — 'Azure fundamentals'; Microsoft Learn — AZ-900 core concepts.
💻 Code: Create a resource group and deploy one small resource three ways — portal, Azure CLI (az), and a Bicep/ARM template — and compare; tag everything by environment.

units.title: Identity & access: Entra ID + RBAC
units.text:
Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is the identity backbone: users, groups, service principals and managed identities. RBAC roles + scopes decide who can do what — the single most important thing to get right, and the most common way cloud gets breached.
🎥 Watch: John Savill — 'Entra ID' and 'Azure RBAC'; Microsoft Learn — RBAC.
💻 Code: Create a service principal and a managed identity; grant a least-privilege RBAC role at resource-group scope; have an app use the managed identity to reach a resource with no stored secret.

units.title: Networking: VNets, NSGs, load balancing
units.text:
Virtual networks, subnets, network security groups (NSGs), public vs private IPs, Azure Load Balancer vs Application Gateway (L7), and private endpoints that lock managed services to your VNet. Most 'why can't it connect' lives here.
🎥 Watch: John Savill — 'Azure networking' masterclass; Microsoft Learn — VNet.
💻 Code: Build a VNet with public + private subnets, NSG rules, a load balancer over two VMs, and a private endpoint to a storage account.

units.title: Compute, storage & managed data (+ Databricks/Fabric)
units.text:
The building blocks: VMs / VM Scale Sets, App Service, Azure Functions (serverless), Azure Storage (blob/files/disks, ADLS), and managed data (Azure SQL, Cosmos DB). This is where my existing Azure Databricks + Microsoft Fabric skills slot in as the lakehouse/analytics layer.
🎥 Watch: John Savill — 'Azure compute options' and 'Azure storage'; Microsoft Learn — Azure Databricks.
💻 Code: Deploy an app on App Service or Functions reading from Blob Storage; connect an Azure Databricks workspace to ADLS and read/write a Delta table — the lakehouse on Azure.

units.title: AKS + Terraform + CI/CD on Azure
units.text:
Managed Kubernetes (AKS) vs the cluster I built by hand — node pools, Entra + ACR integration, and Key Vault for secrets. Terraform (azurerm) provisions it all; CI/CD (GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines) builds -> pushes to ACR -> deploys to AKS.
🎥 Watch: John Savill — 'AKS deep dive'; TechWorld with Nana — 'GitHub Actions / Azure Pipelines to AKS'.
💻 Code: Terraform an AKS cluster + ACR + Key Vault; wire a GitHub Actions (or Azure Pipelines) pipeline that builds an image, pushes to ACR, and deploys to AKS on push.

units.title: Deploy your platform to Azure (Terraform + AKS + CI/CD)
units.text: [Block A] Provision a real Azure footprint as code with Terraform: resource group, VNet + NSGs, AKS, ACR, Key Vault and a storage account (ADLS) — least-privilege via Entra managed identities, no plaintext secrets. [Block B] Ship an app through CI/CD: a pipeline (GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines) that builds, pushes to ACR and deploys to AKS, pulling secrets from Key Vault. [Block C] Tie in the data layer (Azure Databricks / ADLS Delta), add cost tags + a budget alert, and document the architecture — a 'I can run a real cloud platform' piece that plays to my Databricks/Fabric strengths.
units.demo: Cloud platform on Azure: Terraform-provisioned AKS + ACR + Key Vault + ADLS, deployed via CI/CD with least-privilege managed identity.

units.title: The cloud, as a system
units.text: Azure's resource + identity model, VNet networking, managed compute/storage, AKS and Terraform + CI/CD turn 'a Linux box' into a real cloud platform. Re-read my Terraform and confirm every secret comes from Key Vault, not the repo.
units.mastery: Sketch the Azure hierarchy (tenant -> subscription -> resource group -> resource), explain why a managed identity beats a stored secret, and say when I'd reach for AKS over the cluster I built by hand.

units.title: Metrics, logs & traces
units.text:
The three pillars of observability — metrics (what), logs (why), traces (where) — and when to use each.
🎥 Watch: Google SRE book (monitoring); search 'observability three pillars'.
💻 Code: Instrument an app to emit metrics, structured logs and traces for one request path.

units.title: Prometheus & Grafana
units.text:
Metrics collection with Prometheus (scraping, PromQL) and dashboards/alerts with Grafana.
🎥 Watch: TechWorld with Nana — Prometheus/Grafana; search 'Prometheus tutorial'.
💻 Code: Scrape your app's metrics with Prometheus and build a Grafana dashboard for it.

units.title: SLOs, SLIs & error budgets
units.text:
Defining reliability: SLIs (measured), SLOs (targets) and error budgets that balance reliability vs velocity — the heart of SRE.
🎥 Watch: Google SRE book — SLOs; search 'SLI SLO error budget explained'.
💻 Code: Define SLIs + an SLO for your service and compute its error budget from real metrics.

units.title: Alerting & on-call
units.text:
Actionable, symptom-based alerting (not noise), on-call practices, and alert fatigue.
🎥 Watch: Google SRE book — alerting/on-call.
💻 Code: Write symptom-based alerts (latency/error-rate SLO burn) with Alertmanager, not CPU-noise alerts.

units.title: Incident response & postmortems
units.text:
Handling incidents (roles, comms, mitigation) and blameless postmortems that turn failures into improvements.
🎥 Watch: Google SRE book — incident management + postmortems.
💻 Code: Run a game-day: break your service, respond, and write a blameless postmortem.

units.title: Observability & alerting stack for the platform
units.text: [Block A] Instrument your platform (CV/DE/ML/AI services) with metrics, logs and traces; deploy Prometheus + Grafana. [Block B] Define SLIs/SLOs + error budgets and symptom-based alerting for the key user journeys. [Block C] Run a game-day incident and write the postmortem — a portfolio SRE piece that shows operational maturity.

units.title: Running systems reliably
units.text: The three pillars, Prometheus/Grafana, SLOs/error budgets, alerting and incident response are how you run systems like an SRE. Re-read your postmortem.
units.mastery: What's the difference between an SLI, SLO and error budget, and why should alerts be symptom-based?

units.title: perf & eBPF tooling
units.text:
Deep performance analysis: perf, flame graphs, and eBPF (bpftrace/BCC) to observe the kernel + apps with almost no overhead.
🎥 Watch: Brendan Gregg — perf/eBPF; search 'flame graphs explained'.
💻 Code: Profile a CPU-bound app with perf, generate a flame graph, find the hotspot, and try one bpftrace one-liner.

units.title: System & network tuning
units.text:
Finding + fixing bottlenecks across CPU/memory/disk/network using the USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors).
🎥 Watch: Brendan Gregg — the USE method; 'Linux performance tools'.
💻 Code: Apply the USE method to a loaded system, identify the bottleneck resource, and tune it.

units.title: Linux security: SELinux, seccomp
units.text:
Mandatory access control (SELinux/AppArmor), seccomp to restrict syscalls, and defense-in-depth for services/containers.
🎥 Watch: Search 'SELinux explained' and 'seccomp containers'.
💻 Code: Apply a seccomp profile to a container to block dangerous syscalls and observe SELinux/AppArmor denials.

units.title: Hardening & secrets
units.text:
Server/container hardening (least privilege, minimal surface, updates) and secrets hygiene end to end.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux server hardening checklist'; CIS benchmarks.
💻 Code: Run a hardening checklist against your server + containers and fix the top findings.

units.title: Cost & resource accounting
units.text:
Measuring where compute/cost goes (cgroups accounting, cloud cost), right-sizing, and FinOps for infra.
🎥 Watch: Search 'Linux resource accounting cgroups' and cloud cost basics.
💻 Code: Attribute resource usage per service (cgroups/cloud tags) and right-size one over-provisioned component.

units.title: Profile, tune & harden the platform
units.text: [Block A] Profile your platform under load (perf/eBPF, USE method) and fix the top performance bottleneck. [Block B] Harden it: seccomp/AppArmor on containers, a server hardening checklist, least-privilege everywhere. [Block C] Add cost/resource accounting and right-size; document the perf + security + cost wins — a rounded SRE piece.

units.title: Fast and defensible
units.text: perf/eBPF, the USE method, SELinux/seccomp, hardening and cost accounting make systems fast, secure and affordable. Re-read your flame graph.
units.mastery: Walk the USE method to find a bottleneck, and name three ways you'd harden a container running untrusted code.

units.title: Integrate the CV, DE, ML & AI layers
units.text:
Bring the four track capstones together into one intelligent platform: data flows into features, models serve predictions, and a vision + AI layer (document-AI/CV + RAG/agent) sits on top.
🎥 Watch: Review your four capstone architectures and sketch the unified one.
💻 Code: Design + wire the integration: the DE platform feeds the ML models, which feed the vision + AI layer, end to end.

units.title: Deploy on Kubernetes with IaC
units.text:
Deploy the whole platform reproducibly: Terraform for infra, Helm/GitOps for the services.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your K8s + IaC + GitOps work.
💻 Code: Deploy every component to K8s via IaC + GitOps; one command from zero to running.

units.text:
Automated build/test/deploy for the whole platform, with GitOps reconciliation and safe rollouts.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your CI/CD + GitOps work.
💻 Code: Wire CI/CD (test + build + deploy) and GitOps auto-sync for the platform.

units.title: Observability, alerting & SLOs
units.text:
Full-stack observability + SLOs for the integrated platform, so you'd know the moment anything degrades.
🎥 Watch: Reuse your observability/SRE work.
💻 Code: Add metrics/logs/traces, dashboards, SLOs and alerting across the whole platform.

units.text:
Prove it holds up: load testing, chaos/failure injection, and a security pass before you call it production.

units.title: System-design writeup
units.text:
Write the definitive system-design doc for your platform: the problem, architecture, tradeoffs and lessons.
🎥 Watch: Study strong engineering system-design writeups for structure.
💻 Code: Write the full system-design doc (architecture, decisions, tradeoffs, what you'd do next).

units.title: Architecture diagrams
units.text:
Communicate the system visually: clear architecture + data-flow diagrams a stranger can follow.
🎥 Watch: Search 'good architecture diagrams C4 model'.
💻 Code: Produce clean architecture + data-flow diagrams for the platform and every capstone.

units.title: Demo & video walkthrough
units.text:
Show, don't tell: a crisp demo + recorded walkthrough that proves the work is real.

units.title: Blog posts / talks
units.text:
Teach what you built: writeups/talks on the standout projects (GPT from scratch, RAG, the platform) that build your reputation.
🎥 Watch: Study strong engineering blog posts for structure.
💻 Code: Write one deep technical blog post on a flagship project ('I built a GPT/container/platform from scratch').

units.title: Interview & narrative prep
units.text:
Turn the whole journey into a story: the portfolio site, the resume update, and the interview narrative across computer vision, DE, ML, AI and systems.
🎥 Watch: Review your projects and prep the STAR stories.
💻 Code: Update your portfolio + resume and rehearse the 3-minute story for each flagship project.

units.title: Portfolio launch — case studies & demos
units.text: [Block A] Assemble everything: the portfolio site, project case studies, diagrams, demos and blog posts. [Block B] Polish the top 6-8 flagship projects into strong case studies (problem -> approach -> result). [Block C] Launch it publicly (this dashboard, GitHub, LinkedIn) — the capstone of the whole journey and your new professional story.

units.title: Mastery review & what's next
units.text: Writeups, diagrams, demos, blog posts and your narrative turn the whole journey into a career step. Look back at where you started, then decide what you go deep on next.
units.mastery: Deliver your story: who you are now across computer vision, Data Engineering, ML, AI and systems, and the three projects that prove it.
